title: Part 2, Chapter 37
paragraphs: In which the notable adventure of the Distressed Duenna continues

The duke and duchess were delighted to see how readily Don Quixote was falling in with their scheme; but at that point Sancho spoke up. “I just hope this señora duenna doesn’t throw any obstacles in the way of the governorship I’ve been promised, because I once heard an apothecary from Toledo, a man who chattered like a goldfinch, say that wherever duennas got mixed up in things, nothing good could come of it. God bless me, how that apothecary hated them! So the way I figure it, if all duennas, whatever their sort or station, are pests and busybodies, what must the distressed ones be like — this Countess Three-skirts or Three-tails! Because in my country, skirts or tails, tails or skirts, it’s all the same thing.”

“Quiet, friend Sancho,” said Don Quixote. “Since this lady duenna has come looking for me from so distant a land, she cannot be one of those the apothecary had in mind. Besides, this one is a countess, and when countesses serve as duennas, it is in the service of queens and empresses; in their own houses they are absolute mistresses, with other duennas to wait on them.”

To this Doña Rodriguez, who was present, replied, “My lady the duchess has duennas in her service who could be countesses if fortune had willed it so; ‘but laws go the way kings want them to.’ Let no one speak ill of duennas, least of all the old maiden ones — for though I am not one myself, I know perfectly well the advantage a maiden duenna holds over a widowed one; but ‘the man who clipped us has kept hold of the scissors.’”
“Even so,” said Sancho, “there’s so much about duennas that needs clipping, according to my barber, that ‘it’s better not to stir the rice, even if it sticks to the pot.’”

“These squires,” Doña Rodriguez shot back, “are always our enemies. They haunt the antechambers like ghosts and watch our every step, and whenever they are not saying their prayers — which is often enough — they spend their time gossiping about us, digging up our bones and burying our good name. Well, I can tell these walking blockheads that we will go on living in spite of them, and in great houses too, even if we starve and have to cover our flesh, delicate or otherwise, in widow’s black, the way one covers or hides a dunghill on procession day. By my faith, if it were permitted me and there were time enough, I could prove — not only to everyone present here, but to the whole world — that there is no virtue that cannot be found in a duenna.”

“I have no doubt,” said the duchess, “that my good Doña Rodriguez is right, and very much so; but she would do well to wait for the proper moment to fight her own battle and that of all the other duennas, so as to crush the slander of that vile apothecary and uproot the prejudice lodged in the great Sancho Panza’s mind.”
To which Sancho answered, “Ever since I got a whiff of the governorship, I’ve shaken off all the moods of a squire, and I don’t care a wild fig for every duenna in the world.”

They would have carried this dispute about duennas further if they had not heard the fife and drums strike up once more, which told them that the Distressed Duenna was making her entrance. The duchess asked the duke whether it would be proper to go out and receive her, since she was a countess and a person of rank.

“As far as her being a countess goes,” said Sancho, before the duke could answer, “I’m all for your highnesses going out to receive her; but as far as her being a duenna goes, my opinion is that you shouldn’t move a single step.”
“Who asked you to meddle in this, Sancho?” said Don Quixote.

“Who, señor?” said Sancho. “I meddle because I have every right to meddle, as a squire who learned the rules of courtesy in the school of your worship, the most courteous and best-bred knight in the whole world of courtliness. And in these matters, as I’ve heard your worship say, you can lose as much by a card too many as by a card too few — and for a man whose ears are open, a few words are enough.”
“Sancho is right,” said the duke. “We’ll see what sort of woman this countess is, and measure out by that the courtesy she is owed.”

And now the drums and fife came in as they had before; and here the author brought this short chapter to a close and began the next, carrying forward the same adventure, which is one of the most notable in this history.

title: Part 2, Chapter 38
paragraphs: In which the Distressed Duenna tells the story of her misfortunes

After the mournful musicians, as many as twelve duennas filed into the garden in two lines, all wearing wide mourning habits that looked like milled serge, with hoods of fine white gauze so long that only the hem of the robe showed beneath them. Behind them came the Countess Trifaldi, led by the hand by the squire Trifaldin of the White Beard. She was dressed in the finest unnapped black baize — so fine that, had it carried a nap, every tuft would have stood out as big as a Martos chickpea. Her train, or skirt, or whatever the thing ought to be called, ended in three points, each held aloft by the hands of a page, the three pages dressed in mourning as well, so that the three acute angles formed by the three points made an elegant geometrical figure. Everyone who saw the peaked skirt concluded that it must be the reason the countess was called Trifaldi — as if to say, Countess of the Three Skirts — and Benengeli confirms it, adding that her real name was Countess Lobuna, because wolves bred in great numbers in her country; if they had been foxes instead of wolves, she would have been called Countess Zorruna, since it was the custom in those parts for lords to take their distinctive titles from whatever thing or things were most plentiful in their lands. This countess, however, in honor of the new fashion of her skirt, dropped Lobuna and took up Trifaldi.

The twelve duennas and their lady advanced at a processional pace, their faces covered with black veils — not transparent ones like Trifaldin’s, but woven so closely that nothing at all could be seen through them. The moment the company of duennas came fully into view, the duke, the duchess, and Don Quixote rose to their feet, as did everyone else watching the slow-moving procession. The twelve duennas halted and formed a lane, and down it came the Distressed One, with Trifaldin still holding her hand. Seeing this, the duke, the duchess, and Don Quixote walked some twelve paces forward to receive her. Then, kneeling on the ground, she spoke in a voice more hoarse and rough than fine and delicate: “May it please your highnesses not to lavish such courtesies on this your servant — I should say this your handmaid — for I am in such distress that I shall never manage to make a fitting reply, since my strange and unheard-of misfortune has carried off my wits to I know not where; it must be somewhere very far away, because the more I search for them, the less of them I find.”

“The man who failed to see your worth in your very person, señora countess,” said the duke, “would be the one short of wits, for a single glance shows you deserve all the cream of courtesy and the flower of fine breeding.” And raising her by the hand, he led her to a seat beside the duchess, who welcomed her with equal graciousness. Don Quixote kept silent, while Sancho was dying to see the face of Trifaldi and one or two of her many duennas; but there was no chance of that until they chose to unveil themselves of their own accord and free will.

Everyone kept still, waiting to see who would break the silence, and it was the Distressed Duenna who did, in these words: “I am confident, most mighty lord, most beautiful lady, and most discerning company, that my most miserable misery will find in your most valiant breasts a reception no less calm than generous and compassionate, for it is misery enough to melt marble, soften diamonds, and bend the steel of the hardest hearts in the world. But before it is published to your hearing — not to say your ears — I should like to be told whether there is present in this society, circle, or company that knight immaculatissimus, Don Quixote de la Manchissima, and his squirissimus Panza.”

“The Panza is here,” said Sancho before anyone else could answer, “and Don Quixotissimus too; so, most distressedest Duenissima, you may say whatever you wishissimus, for we are all entirely readissimus to do you any servissimus.”

At this Don Quixote rose and addressed the Distressed Duenna: “If your sorrows, afflicted lady, can promise themselves any hope of relief from the valor or strength of any knight-errant, here are mine, which, feeble and limited though they are, shall be devoted entirely to your service. I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, whose calling it is to come to the aid of the needy of every kind; and that being so, señora, you have no need to appeal to anyone’s goodwill or work through preambles — simply tell your troubles plainly and directly, for you are speaking to listeners who will know how to sympathize with them even if they cannot remedy them.”

When she heard this, the Distressed Duenna made as if to throw herself at Don Quixote’s feet — and in fact she did fall before them, and said, struggling to embrace them, “Before these feet and these legs I cast myself, O unconquered knight, for they are what they are: the foundations and pillars of knight-errantry. These feet I long to kiss, for upon their steps hangs and depends the only remedy for my misfortune, O valorous errant, whose true achievements leave behind and eclipse the fabled ones of the Amadises, the Esplandians, and the Belianises!” Then, turning from Don Quixote to Sancho Panza and seizing his hands, she said, “O you, the most loyal squire that ever served a knight-errant in this present age or in ages past, whose goodness stretches further than the beard of my companion Trifaldin here present, well may you boast that in serving the great Don Quixote you are serving, gathered into one, the whole host of knights that have ever borne arms in this world. I implore you, by what you owe to your most loyal goodness, to be my kind intercessor with your master, so that he may swiftly come to the aid of this most humble and most unfortunate countess.”

To this Sancho answered, “As for my goodness, señora, being as long and as great as your squire’s beard — that matters very little to me. May my soul be well bearded and mustached when it comes time to leave this life; that is what counts. About beards down here I care little or nothing. But without all these blandishments and pleadings, I will ask my master — for I know he loves me, and besides, he needs me just now for a certain piece of business — to help and favor your worship as far as he can. So unpack your woes and lay them out before us, and leave the rest to us, for we shall all be of one mind.”

The duke and duchess, who had set up this whole adventure themselves, were ready to burst with laughter at all of it, and between themselves they praised how cleverly the Trifaldi played her part. Returning to her seat, she said, “Over the famous kingdom of Kandy, which lies between the great Trapobana and the Southern Sea, two leagues beyond Cape Comorin, reigned Queen Doña Maguncia, widow of King Archipiela, her lord and husband. From their marriage came the Princess Antonomasia, heiress to the kingdom, and this Princess Antonomasia was raised and educated under my care and direction, since I was the oldest and highest-ranking of her mother’s duennas. Time went by, and young Antonomasia reached the age of fourteen with such perfect beauty that nature could not have raised it higher. Nor should anyone suppose her mind was a child’s: she was as intelligent as she was beautiful, and she was more beautiful than anyone in the world — and still is, unless the envious fates and the three hard-hearted sisters have cut her thread of life. They have not, though, for Heaven would never allow so great a wrong to Earth as plucking, unripe, the grapes of the loveliest vineyard on its surface. Countless princes, not only of her own country but of others, fell in love with this beauty, to which my poor feeble tongue cannot do justice; and among them a private gentleman at the court dared to lift his thoughts to the heaven of such loveliness, trusting in his youth, his gallant bearing, his many talents and graces, and his quick and ready wit. For I may tell your highnesses, if it does not weary you, that he played the guitar so that it fairly spoke; he was a poet besides, and a fine dancer; and he could build birdcages so well that he might have earned his living by making them alone, had he ever been reduced to utter poverty — and gifts and graces of that kind are enough to bring down a mountain, never mind a tender young girl. But all his gallantry, wit, and gaiety, all his talents and accomplishments, would have done him little or no good toward taking the fortress of my pupil if the shameless thief had not first taken the precaution of capturing me. First the villain, the heartless vagabond, set out to win my goodwill and buy my consent, so that I, like a treacherous gatekeeper, would hand him the keys of the fortress I was set to guard. In short, he worked his way into my mind and broke down my resolve with I know not what trinkets and jewels he gave me; but what made me give way more than anything else, what brought about my fall, was some verses I heard him singing one night from a grated window that opened onto the street where he lived. If I remember rightly, they ran like this:

From that sweet enemy of mine
my bleeding heart has taken its wound;
and to make the torment greater, I am bound
to suffer it and give no sign.

The lines seemed pearls to me, and his voice sweet as syrup; and afterwards — indeed ever since, looking at the misfortune I fell into through them — I have thought that poets ought to be banished from all well-governed states, as Plato advised: at least the love poets, for they write verses not like those of ‘The Marquis of Mantua,’ which delight women and children and draw their tears, but sharp-pointed conceits that pierce the heart like soft thorns and strike it like lightning, leaving the clothing untouched. Another time he sang:

Come, Death, but come so veiled and still
that I never feel your approach, the how or when,
lest the discovery of how sweet it is to die
should bring me back to life again.

—and other verses and refrains of the same kind, the sort that enchant when they are sung and fascinate when they are written down. And then, when these poets condescend to compose a kind of verse that was fashionable in Kandy at the time, the kind they call seguidillas! That is when hearts leap and laughter bursts out, when the body grows restless and all the senses turn to quicksilver. And so I say, sirs, that such troubadours richly deserve to be banished to the isles of the lizards. Though the fault is not really theirs, but belongs to the simpletons who praise them and the fools who believe in them; and had I been the faithful duenna I should have been, his stale conceits would never have moved me, nor would I have been taken in by phrases like ‘in death I live,’ ‘in ice I burn,’ ‘in flames I shiver,’ ‘hopeless I hope,’ ‘I go and I stay,’ and the other paradoxes of that sort their writings are stuffed with. And then, when they promise the Phœnix of Arabia, the crown of Ariadne, the horses of the Sun, the pearls of the South, the gold of Tibar, and the balsam of Panchaia! That is when they let their pens run loose, since it costs them nothing to make promises they have no intention — and no power — of keeping. But where am I wandering off to? Woe is me, unlucky creature! What madness or folly leads me to recite other people’s faults when there is so much to be said about my own? Again, woe is me, wretched that I am! It was not the verses that conquered me but my own simplicity; it was not the music that made me yield but my own imprudence; my great ignorance and small caution opened the road and cleared the path for the advances of Don Clavijo — for that was the name of the gentleman I have been speaking of. And so, with me serving as go-between, he found his way many a time into the chamber of the deceived Antonomasia — deceived not by him but by me — under the title of lawful husband; for sinner though I am, I would never have let him come near the edge of her shoe-sole without being her husband first. No, no — in any business of this kind that I take in hand, marriage must come first. There was just one snag in this case, the inequality of rank: Don Clavijo was a private gentleman, and the Princess Antonomasia, as I said, heiress to the kingdom. For some time the entanglement stayed secret, hidden by the precautions of my cunning, until I saw that a certain swelling of Antonomasia’s waist must before long give it away. Dreading this, we all took counsel together there, and it was agreed that before the mischief came to light, Don Clavijo should claim Antonomasia as his wife before the Vicar, on the strength of a written promise of marriage the princess had given him — drafted by my wit in terms so binding that the strength of Samson himself could not have broken them. The necessary steps were taken; the Vicar saw the agreement and heard the lady’s confession; she confessed everything in full, and he ordered her into the custody of a very respectable alguacil of the court.”

“So there are alguacils of the court in Kandy too,” said Sancho at this point, “and poets, and seguidillas? I swear the world must be one and the same everywhere! But hurry along, Señora Trifaldi, for it is getting late and I am dying to know the end of this long story.”
“That I will,” answered the countess.

title: Part 2, Chapter 39
paragraphs: In which the Trifaldi continues her marvelous and memorable story

Every word out of Sancho's mouth delighted the duchess as much as it drove Don Quixote to despair. He ordered him to be quiet, and the Distressed One continued: “In the end, after a great deal of questioning and answering, since the princess stuck to her story and never changed or backed away from her original declaration, the Vicar ruled in Don Clavijo's favor, and she was handed over to him as his lawful wife. Queen Doña Maguncia, Princess Antonomasia's mother, took this so much to heart that within three days we had buried her.”
“She must have died, then,” said Sancho.
“Naturally,” said Trifaldin; “in Kandy they don't bury people alive, only the dead ones.”

“Señor Squire,” said Sancho, “people in a faint have been buried before now because everyone believed they were dead, and it seems to me Queen Maguncia should have settled for fainting instead of dying. While there's life, a great many things sort themselves out, and the princess's blunder wasn't so terrible that she needed to take it so hard. If the lady had married one of her pages, or some other servant of the household, as plenty of others have done, from what I hear, then the damage would have been beyond repair. But marrying a gentleman as polished and accomplished as the one just described to us—honestly, truly, even if it was a foolish thing to do, it wasn't nearly as foolish as you think. By my master's own rules here—and he won't let me tell a lie—just as men of letters are made into bishops, so gentlemen knights, especially the errant kind, can be made into kings and emperors.”

“You are right, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “for if a knight-errant has even two fingers' width of good luck, he stands every chance of becoming the greatest lord on earth. But let señora the Distressed One go on, for I suspect she still has the bitter part of this so-far-sweet story to tell us.”

“The bitter part is indeed still to come,” said the countess, “and bitter enough to make colocynth taste sweet and oleander seem delicious by comparison. Well then, the queen being truly dead and not merely in a faint, we buried her; and we had scarcely covered her with earth, scarcely spoken our last farewells, when—_quis talia fando temperet a lachrymis?_—there appeared above the queen's grave, mounted on a wooden horse, the giant Malambruno, Maguncia's first cousin, a man who is not only cruel but an enchanter as well. To avenge his cousin's death, to punish Don Clavijo's audacity, and out of fury at Antonomasia's defiance, he used his arts to enchant them both right there on the grave: she was turned into a brass ape, and he into a hideous crocodile of some unknown metal, while between the two there stands a pillar, likewise of metal, inscribed with certain characters in the Syriac language, which, translated into Kandian and now into Castilian, read as follows: ‘These two reckless lovers shall not regain their former shapes until the valiant Manchegan comes to meet me in single combat, for the Fates have reserved this unprecedented adventure for his great valor alone.’ When this was done, he drew an enormous broad scimitar from its sheath, seized me by the hair, and made as if to slit my throat and cut my head clean off. I was paralyzed with terror, my voice froze in my throat, and I was in utter anguish; even so I gathered what strength I could and, in a trembling, pitiful voice, said such things to him that I persuaded him to hold back from carrying out so harsh a punishment. He then had all the duennas of the palace—the ones you see here—brought before him, and after dwelling on the enormity of our offense, and railing against duennas, their characters, their wicked habits and still worse schemes, blaming all of them for what I alone had done, he declared that he would not put us to death, but would inflict slower punishments on us that would amount to perpetual civil death; and the very moment he stopped speaking, we all felt the pores of our faces opening and stinging, as though pricked with needle points. We immediately put our hands to our faces and found ourselves in the condition you see now.”

At this the Distressed One and the other duennas lifted the veils that covered them and revealed faces all bristling with beards—some red, some black, some white, and some gray—a sight at which the duke and duchess made a show of astonishment. Don Quixote and Sancho were dumbfounded, and the onlookers struck speechless, while the Trifaldi continued: “This is how that malicious villain Malambruno punished us, covering the softness and delicacy of our faces with these coarse bristles! If only heaven had let him strike off our heads with that enormous scimitar of his instead of darkening the light of our faces with this wool-stubble that covers us! For consider the matter, sirs—and what I am about to say I would say with my eyes streaming like fountains, except that the thought of our misfortune, and the oceans they have already wept, keep them as dry as barley stalks, so I say it without tears—where, I ask you, can a duenna with a beard go? What father or mother will take pity on her? Who will come to her aid? If even with a smooth complexion, and a face tormented by a thousand kinds of lotions and cosmetics, she can scarcely find anyone to love her, what is she to do when she shows a face that has turned into a thicket? Oh duennas, my companions! We were born in an unlucky moment, and it was an ill-starred hour when our fathers begot us!” And with these words she seemed about to faint.

title: Part 2, Chapter 40
paragraphs: About matters relating and belonging to this adventure and to this memorable history

Truly, everyone who takes pleasure in histories like this one ought to be grateful to Cide Hamete, its original author, for the scrupulous care he has taken to lay before us every minute detail, leaving out nothing — however trifling — that he doesn't make plain and clear. He sketches the thoughts, unveils the daydreams, answers questions before they're asked, settles doubts, disposes of objections, and in a word makes plain the smallest points the most inquisitive reader could want to know. O renowned author! O lucky Don Quixote! O famous, famous, droll Sancho! Long may you all live, every one of you, for the delight and amusement of the inhabitants of the earth!

The history goes on to say that when Sancho saw the Distressed One faint, he exclaimed, "I swear by the faith of an honest man, and by the shades of all my Panza ancestors, that I have never seen or heard of, nor has my master ever recounted or even imagined, an adventure like this. A thousand devils — not that I'd curse you — take you, Malambruno, for an enchanter and a giant! Could you find no other sort of punishment for these poor sinners but bearding them? Wouldn't it have been better — better for them — to take off half their noses from the bridge up, even if it left them snuffling when they spoke, than to plant beards on them? I'll bet they haven't the means to pay anyone to shave them."

"That is the truth, señor," said one of the twelve. "We have no money to get ourselves shaved, and so some of us have taken to using sticking-plasters as a cheap remedy — applied to the face and ripped off with a jerk, they leave us as bare and smooth as the bottom of a stone mortar. There are, to be sure, women in Kandy who go from house to house removing down, trimming eyebrows, and making cosmetics for the ladies; but we, the duennas of my lady, would never let them in, for most of them have the air of go-betweens who were once principals themselves. Unless we are relieved by Señor Don Quixote, we shall be carried to our graves bearded."
"I will pluck out my own in the land of the Moors," said Don Quixote, "if I don't cure yours."

At this the Trifaldi recovered from her swoon and said, "The chime of that promise, valiant knight, reached my ears in the depths of my fainting fit, and was enough to revive me and bring back my senses. So once again I implore you, illustrious knight-errant, indomitable sir, to let your gracious promises be turned into deeds."
"There shall be no delay on my part," said Don Quixote. "Consider, señora, what it is I must do, for my heart is more than ready to serve you."

"The fact is," replied the Distressed One, "it is five thousand leagues, give or take a couple, from here to the kingdom of Kandy if you go by land — but only three thousand two hundred and twenty-seven if you go through the air in a straight line. You must know, too, that Malambruno told me that whenever fate provided the knight to deliver us, he himself would send him a steed far better and less skittish than any post-horse; for it will be the very wooden horse on which the valiant Pierres carried off the fair Magalona — a horse guided by a peg in its forehead that serves as a bridle, and which flies through the air so fast you would think the devils themselves were driving it. According to ancient tradition, this horse was made by Merlin. He lent it to Pierres, who was a friend of his and took long journeys on it, and (as I said) carried off the fair Magalona, bearing her through the air on its haunches and making everyone who watched them from below gape in astonishment. He never lent it except to those he loved or those who paid him well; and since the great Pierres, no one is known to have mounted it — until now. Malambruno stole it from him by his magic art, and now he has it in his possession, using it for the journeys he constantly makes through different parts of the world. He is here today, in France tomorrow, and in Potosí the day after; and the best of it is that this horse neither eats nor sleeps nor wears out shoes, and goes at an ambling pace through the air without wings, so that whoever rides on it can carry a full cup of water in his hand without spilling a drop — that's how smoothly and easily it goes. Which is why the fair Magalona enjoyed riding it so much."
"For going smoothly and easily," said Sancho at this, "give me my Dapple. He can't go through the air, but on the ground I'll back him against all the amblers in the world."

They all laughed, and the Distressed One continued, "And this same horse, if Malambruno is disposed to put an end to our sufferings, will be here before us within half an hour after nightfall; for he announced to me that the sign by which I would know I had found the right knight would be his sending me the horse — wherever the knight might be — swiftly and promptly."
"And how many is there room for on this horse?" Sancho asked.
"Two," said the Distressed One. "One in the saddle, the other on the croup; usually a knight and his squire, when there is no damsel being carried off."
"I'd like to know, Señora Distressed One," said Sancho, "what the name of this horse is."

"His name," said the Distressed One, "is not the same as Bellerophon's horse Pegasus, or Alexander the Great's Bucephalus, or Orlando Furioso's Brigliador, nor Bayard, the horse of Reinaldos of Montalbán, nor Frontino like Ruggiero's, nor Boötes or Peritoa, as they say the horses of the sun were called; nor is he called Orelia, like the horse on which the unfortunate Rodrigo, the last king of the Goths, rode to the battle where he lost his life and his kingdom."

"I'll bet," said Sancho, "that since they have given him none of these famous names of well-known horses, they also haven't given him the name of my master's Rocinante — which for being fit beats all the rest mentioned."

"That is true," said the bearded countess, "but it suits him very well, for he is called Clavileño the Swift — a name that fits his being made of wood, and the swift pace at which he travels. So as far as names go, he can stand comparison with the famous Rocinante."
"I've no objection to the name," said Sancho. "But with what kind of bridle or halter is he managed?"

"I have said already," said the Trifaldi, "that it is by a peg — by turning it one way or the other, the knight who rides him makes him go as he pleases: through the upper air, or skimming and almost sweeping the ground, or in that middle course which is sought and followed in all well-regulated proceedings."

"I'd like to see him," said Sancho. "But to imagine I'm going to mount him, in the saddle or on the croup, is to ask pears of the elm tree. A good joke! I can barely keep my seat on Dapple, on a pack-saddle softer than silk itself, and here they'd have me hold on to plank haunches with no pad or cushion of any kind! Heavens, I have no intention of bruising myself to shave anyone's beard; let each woman shave herself as best she can. I'm not going to accompany my master on any such long journey. Besides, I can't help with shaving these beards the way I can with disenchanting my lady Dulcinea."
"Yes you can, my friend," replied the Trifaldi; "so much so that without you, as I understand it, we can do nothing."

"In the king's name!" exclaimed Sancho. "What have squires to do with the adventures of their masters? Are they to have the fame of what they go through, while we get the labour? Body of me! If the historians would only say, 'Such and such a knight finished such and such an adventure, but with the help of so-and-so his squire, without whom it would have been impossible,' — but no, they write curtly: 'Don Paralipomenon of the Three Stars accomplished the adventure of the six monsters,' without mentioning such a person as his squire, who was there the whole time, as if there were no such being. Once more, sirs, I say my master may go alone, and much good may it do him; I'll stay here in the company of my lady the duchess; and maybe by the time he comes back, he will find the lady Dulcinea's affair much advanced — for I mean, in leisure hours and idle moments, to give myself a spell of whipping that won't leave a hair to cover me."

"For all that, you must go if it's necessary, my good Sancho," said the duchess; "they are worthy folk who ask you, and the faces of these ladies must not remain overgrown like this because of your idle fears — that would be a hard case indeed."

"In the king's name, once more!" said Sancho. "If this charitable work were being done for the sake of damsels in convents or for charity-school girls, a man might expose himself to some hardship; but to put up with it for the sake of stripping beards off duennas! Devil take it! I'd sooner see them all bearded, from the highest to the lowest, and from the most prudish to the most affected."

"You are very hard on duennas, Sancho my friend," said the duchess. "You lean rather heavily toward the opinion of the Toledo apothecary. But you are wrong: there are duennas in my house who would serve as model duennas; and here is my Doña Rodríguez, who won't let me say otherwise."

"Your excellency may say it if you like," said the Rodríguez, "for God knows the truth of everything; and whether we duennas are good or bad, bearded or smooth, we are our mothers' daughters like other women; and as God sent us into the world, he knows why, and on his mercy I rely, not on anybody's beard."

"Well, Señora Rodríguez, Señora Trifaldi, and present company," said Don Quixote, "I trust Heaven will look on your troubles with kindly eyes, for Sancho will do as I bid him. Only let Clavileño come, and let me find myself face to face with Malambruno, and I am certain no razor will shave you more easily than my sword will shave Malambruno's head off his shoulders — for 'God bears with the wicked, but not forever.'"

"Ah!" exclaimed the Distressed One at this. "May all the stars of the celestial regions look down on your greatness with benign eyes, valiant knight, and shed every prosperity and valour upon your heart, that it may be the shield and safeguard of the abused and downtrodden race of duennas, detested by apothecaries, sneered at by squires, and made fun of by pages. Cursed be the girl who, in the flower of her youth, would not sooner become a nun than a duenna! Unfortunate beings that we are, we duennas! Even if we are descended in the direct male line from Hector of Troy himself, our mistresses still address us as 'you,' if they think it makes queens of them. O giant Malambruno, though you are an enchanter, you are true to your promises. Send us now the peerless Clavileño, that our misfortune may be brought to an end; for if hot weather sets in and these beards of ours are still here, alas for our lot!"

The Trifaldi said this so pitifully that she drew tears from everyone's eyes, and even Sancho's filled up; and he resolved in his heart to accompany his master to the furthest ends of the earth, if the removal of the wool from those venerable faces depended on it.

title: Part 2, Chapter 41
paragraphs: About the arrival of Clavileño and the end of this protracted adventure

And now night came, and with it the appointed hour for the arrival of the famous horse Clavileño, whose non-appearance was already beginning to make Don Quixote uneasy. It struck him that since Malambruno was taking so long to send the horse, either he was not the knight the adventure was reserved for, or else Malambruno did not dare meet him in single combat. But lo! suddenly four wild men, all clad in green ivy, came into the garden carrying a great wooden horse on their shoulders. They stood it on the ground, and one of the wild men said, "Let the knight with the heart for it mount this machine."
Here Sancho exclaimed, "I don't mount it, for I have neither the heart nor am I a knight."

"And let the squire, if he has one," the wild man went on, "take his seat on the croup, and let him trust the valiant Malambruno; for by no sword but his, nor by the malice of any other, shall he be attacked. He need only turn this peg in the horse's neck, and the horse will bear them through the air to where Malambruno awaits them. But, so that the great altitude of their flight doesn't make them giddy, their eyes must be covered until the horse neighs, which will be the sign that they have completed their journey."

With these words, leaving Clavileño behind, they retired with easy dignity the way they had come. As soon as the Distressed One saw the horse, almost in tears she exclaimed to Don Quixote, "Valiant knight, the promise of Malambruno has proved trustworthy. The horse has come, our beards are growing, and by every hair in them, every one of us implores you to shave and shear us — it is only a matter of mounting him with your squire and making a happy beginning to your new journey."

"That I will, Señora Countess Trifaldi," said Don Quixote, "most gladly and with the heartiest goodwill, without even stopping to take a cushion or put on my spurs, so as not to lose time — such is my desire to see you and all these duennas shaved clean."

"That I won't," said Sancho, "willingly or unwillingly, in any shape or form. And if this shaving can't be done without my mounting on the croup, my master had better look out for another squire to go with him, and these ladies for some other way of smoothing their faces. I'm no witch, with a taste for travelling through the air. What would my islanders say when they heard their governor was off strolling around on the winds? And another thing: as it is three thousand-odd leagues from here to Kandy, if the horse gets tired or the giant takes offence, we'll be half a dozen years getting back, and there won't be an isle or island in the world that will know me. As the common saying goes, 'in delay there's danger,' and 'when they offer you a heifer, run with a halter' — these ladies' beards must excuse me. 'Saint Peter is very well in Rome' — meaning I am very well in this house where so much is made of me, and I'm hoping for such a good thing from the master as to see myself a governor."

"Friend Sancho," said the duke at this, "the island I have promised you is not a moving one, nor one that will run away. It has roots so deeply buried in the bowels of the earth that it will be no easy matter to pluck it up or shift it from where it is. You know as well as I do that there is no important office that isn't obtained by some sort of bribe, great or small. Well, what I expect to receive for this governorship is that you go with your master Don Quixote and bring this memorable adventure to a conclusion. Whether you return on Clavileño as quickly as his speed seems to promise, or adverse fortune brings you back on foot, travelling as a pilgrim from hostel to hostel and inn to inn, you will always find your island on your return exactly where you left it, and your islanders with the same eagerness they have always had to receive you as their governor, and my goodwill the same. Doubt not the truth of this, Señor Sancho, for that would be grievously wronging my disposition to serve you."

"Say no more, señor," said Sancho. "I am a poor squire and not up to carrying so much courtesy. Let my master mount, bandage my eyes, and commit me to God's care; and tell me if I may commend myself to our Lord or call on the angels to protect me when we go towering up there."

To this the Trifaldi answered, "Sancho, you may freely commend yourself to God or to whomever you like; for Malambruno, though an enchanter, is a Christian, and works his enchantments with great circumspection, taking very good care not to fall out with anyone."
"Well then," said Sancho, "may God and the most holy Trinity of Gaeta help me!"

"Since the memorable adventure of the fulling mills," said Don Quixote, "I have never seen Sancho in such a fright as he is now; were I as superstitious as some, his abject fear would cause me some little uneasiness of spirit. But come here, Sancho — with the leave of these gentlefolk, I would say a word or two to you in private." Drawing Sancho aside among the trees of the garden and seizing both his hands, he said, "You see, brother Sancho, the long journey ahead of us; God knows when we will return, or what leisure or opportunity this business will allow us. So I want you to retire to your chamber now, as though you were going to fetch something needed for the road, and in a moment give yourself, even if only five hundred lashes, on account of the three thousand three hundred you are bound to deliver. It will be all to the good; to make a beginning with a thing is to have it half finished."

"By God," said Sancho, "your worship must be out of your senses! This is like the common saying, 'You see me with child, and you want me a virgin.' Just as I'm about to go sit on a bare board, your worship would have me score my backside! Indeed, your worship is not being reasonable. Let's be off to shave these duennas, and on our return I promise on my word to make such haste to wipe off all that's owed that it will satisfy your worship. I can't say more than that."
"Well, I'll comfort myself with that promise, my good Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "and I believe you will keep it; for though stupid, you are truthful."
"I'm not voracious," said Sancho, "only peckish; but even if I was a little, still I'd keep my word."

With this they went back to mount Clavileño, and as they were about to do so Don Quixote said, "Cover your eyes, Sancho, and mount; for one who sends for us from such distant lands cannot mean to deceive us for the paltry glory of tricking people who trust him. Even if everything turned out the opposite of what I hope, no malice could dim the glory of having undertaken this exploit."

"Let us be off, señor," said Sancho. "I have taken the beards and tears of these ladies deeply to heart, and I won't enjoy a bite of food until I have seen them restored to their former smoothness. Mount, your worship, and blindfold yourself; for if I am to go on the croup, it's plain the rider in the saddle must mount first."

"That is true," said Don Quixote; and taking a handkerchief out of his pocket, he asked the Distressed One to bandage his eyes very carefully. But after having them bandaged he uncovered them again, saying, "If my memory doesn't deceive me, I have read in Virgil of the Palladium of Troy, a wooden horse the Greeks offered to the goddess Pallas, which was filled with armed knights who later destroyed Troy. So it would be just as well to see, first of all, what Clavileño has in his stomach."

"There is no need," said the Distressed One. "I will be his guarantor — I know that Malambruno has nothing tricky or treacherous about him. You may mount without any fear, Señor Don Quixote; on my head be it if any harm comes to you."

Don Quixote thought that to say anything further about his safety would put his courage in an unfavourable light; and so, without another word, he mounted Clavileño and tried the peg, which turned easily. Since he had no stirrups and his legs hung down, he looked like nothing so much as a figure in some Roman triumph painted or embroidered on a Flemish tapestry.

Much against the grain, and very slowly, Sancho proceeded to mount; and after settling himself as well as he could on the croup, he found it rather hard and not at all soft, and asked the duke if he could oblige him with a pad of some kind, or a cushion — even if it were off the couch of his lady the duchess, or the bed of one of the pages — as the haunches of that horse were more like marble than wood. At this the Trifaldi observed that Clavileño would not bear any kind of harness or trappings, and that his best bet would be to sit sideways like a woman, since that way he would not feel the hardness so much.

Sancho did so, and, bidding everyone farewell, allowed his eyes to be bandaged, but immediately uncovered them again. Looking tenderly and tearfully on those in the garden, he begged them to help him in his present strait with plenty of Paternosters and Ave Marias, that God might provide someone to say as many for them, whenever they found themselves in a similar emergency.

At this Don Quixote exclaimed, "Are you on the gallows, thief, or at your last moment, that you use such pitiful entreaties? Cowardly, spiritless creature, are you not in the very place the fair Magalona occupied, and from which she descended — not into the grave, but to become Queen of France, unless the histories lie? And I, who am here beside you, may I not put myself on a par with the valiant Pierres, who pressed this very spot I now press? Cover your eyes, cover your eyes, abject animal, and let not your fear escape your lips, at least in my presence."
"Blindfold me," said Sancho. "Since you won't let me commend myself or be commended to God, is it any wonder I'm afraid there's a region of devils around here that will carry us off to Peralvillo?"

They were then blindfolded; and Don Quixote, finding himself settled to his satisfaction, felt for the peg. The instant he placed his fingers on it, all the duennas and everyone standing by lifted up their voices exclaiming, "God guide you, valiant knight! God be with you, intrepid squire! Now, now you go cleaving the air more swiftly than an arrow! Now you begin to amaze and astonish everyone gazing at you from the earth! Take care not to wobble, valiant Sancho! Mind you don't fall, for your fall will be worse than that rash youth's who tried to steer his father the Sun's chariot!"

As Sancho heard the voices, clinging tightly to his master and winding his arms around him, he said, "Señor, how do they make out that we are going up so high, if their voices reach us here and they sound as if they're speaking right next to us?"

"Don't mind that, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "In affairs of this kind, flights like this being out of the ordinary course of things, you can see and hear as much as you like a thousand leagues away. But don't squeeze me so tight, or you'll upset me; and really, I don't know what you have to be uneasy or frightened about, for I can safely swear I never mounted a smoother-going steed in all my life — one would think we never stirred from one place. Banish fear, my friend, for everything is going as it should, and we have the wind at our backs."

"That's true," said Sancho, "for such a strong wind is coming at me from this side that it feels as if people were blowing on me with a thousand pairs of bellows." Which was the case: they were puffing at him with a great pair of bellows. The whole adventure was so well planned by the duke, the duchess, and their majordomo that nothing was left out to make it perfectly successful.

Now Don Quixote, feeling the blast, said, "Beyond a doubt, Sancho, we must already have reached the second region of the air, where the hail and snow are generated. The thunder, the lightning, and the thunderbolts are generated in the third region; and if we go on rising at this rate, we will shortly plunge into the region of fire, and I don't know how to regulate this peg so as not to mount up where we will be burned."

Just then they began to warm their faces, from a distance, with tow that could easily be set on fire and put out again, fixed on the end of a cane. Feeling the heat, Sancho said, "May I die if we are not already in that fire region, or very near it — a good part of my beard has been singed, and I have a mind, señor, to uncover and see whereabouts we are."

"Do nothing of the kind," said Don Quixote. "Remember the true story of the licentiate Torralba, whom the devils carried flying through the air on a stick with his eyes shut; who in twelve hours reached Rome and dismounted at Torre di Nona, a street in the city, and saw the whole sack and storming and the death of Bourbon, and was back in Madrid the next morning, where he gave an account of all he had seen. He said, moreover, that as he was passing through the air the devil told him to open his eyes, and he did so, and saw himself so near the body of the moon, or so it seemed to him, that he could have laid hold of it with his hand; and that he didn't dare look at the earth lest he be seized with giddiness. So, Sancho, we'd best not uncover ourselves; the one who has us in charge will be responsible for us. Perhaps we are gaining altitude and rising so as to descend at one swoop on the kingdom of Kandy, as the saker or falcon does on the heron, so as to seize it however high it may soar. And though it seems to us not half an hour since we left the garden, believe me, we must have travelled a great distance."
"I don't know about that," said Sancho; "all I know is that if Señora Magallanes or Magalona was satisfied with this croup, she could not have been very tender of flesh."

The duke, the duchess, and everyone in the garden were listening to the conversation of the two heroes, and were enormously amused by it. Now, wanting to put a finishing touch on this rare and well-contrived adventure, they applied a light to Clavileño's tail with some tow; and the horse, being full of squibs and crackers, immediately blew up with a tremendous noise and brought Don Quixote and Sancho Panza to the ground half singed. By this time the bearded band of duennas, the Trifaldi and all, had vanished from the garden, and those who remained lay stretched on the ground as if in a swoon. Don Quixote and Sancho got up rather shaken, and looking about them, were filled with amazement at finding themselves in the same garden they had started from, and at seeing such a number of people stretched on the ground. Their astonishment was increased when, at one side of the garden, they spotted a tall lance planted in the ground, and hanging from it by two cords of green silk a smooth white parchment with the following inscription in large gold letters: "The illustrious knight Don Quixote of La Mancha has, by merely attempting it, finished and concluded the adventure of the Countess Trifaldi, otherwise called the Distressed Duenna. Malambruno is now satisfied on every point, the chins of the duennas are smooth and clean, and King Don Clavijo and Queen Antonomasia are restored to their original form; and when the squirely flagellation has been completed, the white dove shall find herself delivered from the pestiferous gerfalcons that persecute her, and in the arms of her beloved mate; for such is the decree of the sage Merlin, arch-enchanter of enchanters."

As soon as Don Quixote had read the inscription on the parchment, he saw clearly that it referred to the disenchantment of Dulcinea. Returning hearty thanks to heaven that he had with so little danger achieved so grand an exploit as restoring the faces of those venerable duennas to their former complexion, he advanced towards the duke and duchess, who had not yet come to themselves. Taking the duke by the hand, he said, "Be of good cheer, worthy sir, be of good cheer; it's nothing at all; the adventure is over and without any harm done, as the inscription on this post plainly shows."

The duke came to slowly, like one recovering consciousness after a heavy sleep; the duchess and everyone else who had fallen prostrate about the garden did the same, with such displays of wonder and amazement that they would almost have convinced anyone that what they so adroitly pretended in jest had really happened to them. The duke read the placard with half-shut eyes, then ran to embrace Don Quixote with open arms, declaring him the best knight ever seen in any age. Sancho kept looking around for the Distressed One, to see what her face was like without the beard, and whether she was as beautiful as her elegant figure promised; but they told him that the instant Clavileño descended flaming through the air and hit the ground, the whole band of duennas with the Trifaldi vanished, and that they were already shaved and without a stump left.

The duchess asked Sancho how he had fared on that long journey, to which Sancho replied, "I felt, señora, that we were flying through the region of fire, as my master told me, and I wanted to uncover my eyes for a bit. But my master, when I asked leave to uncover myself, wouldn't let me. Since I have a little curiosity in me and a desire to know what is forbidden and kept from me, quietly and without anyone seeing me, I drew aside the handkerchief covering my eyes ever so little, close to my nose, and from underneath I looked toward the earth, and it seemed to me it was no bigger than a grain of mustard seed, and that the men walking on it were little bigger than hazel nuts; so you can see how high we must have got by then."

To this the duchess said, "Sancho, my friend, watch what you're saying. It seems you couldn't have seen the earth — only the men walking on it; for if the earth looked to you like a grain of mustard seed and each man like a hazel nut, one man alone would have covered the whole earth."
"That is true," said Sancho, "but even so I got a glimpse of a bit of one side of it, and I saw it all."
"Take care, Sancho," said the duchess; "from a glimpse of one side, one doesn't see the whole of what one is looking at."

"I don't understand that way of looking at things," said Sancho. "All I know is that your ladyship would do well to bear in mind that since we were flying by enchantment, I could just as well have seen the whole earth and all the men by enchantment, whichever way I looked. And if you won't believe this, no more will you believe that, uncovering myself nearly to the eyebrows, I saw myself so close to the sky that there wasn't a palm and a half between me and it; and by everything I can swear by, señora, it is mighty big! And it so happened we came by where the seven goats are, and by God and upon my soul, since in my youth I was a goatherd in my own country, as soon as I saw them I felt a longing to be among them for a little while, and if I had not given in to it I think I'd have burst. So I come and act, and what do I do? without saying anything to anybody, not even my master, softly and quietly I got down from Clavileño and amused myself with the goats — which are like violets, like flowers — for nearly three-quarters of an hour; and Clavileño never stirred or moved an inch."
"And while the good Sancho was amusing himself with the goats," said the duke, "how did Señor Don Quixote amuse himself?"

To which Don Quixote replied, "Since all these things and such occurrences are outside the ordinary course of nature, it is no wonder Sancho says what he does. For my own part, I can only say I did not uncover my eyes either above or below, and I saw neither sky nor earth nor sea nor shore. It is true I felt I was passing through the region of the air, and even that I touched that of fire; but that we went farther than that I cannot believe. The region of fire being between the heaven of the moon and the last region of the air, we could not have reached that heaven where Sancho says the seven goats are without being burned; and since we were not burned, either Sancho is lying or Sancho is dreaming."
"I am neither lying nor dreaming," said Sancho. "Just ask me what those goats looked like, and you'll see by that whether I'm telling the truth or not."
"Tell us, then, Sancho," said the duchess.
"Two of them," said Sancho, "are green, two blood-red, two blue, and one a mixture of all colours."
"An odd sort of goat, that," said the duke. "In this earthly region of ours we have no such colours — I mean goats of such colours."
"That's plain enough," said Sancho. "Of course there must be a difference between the goats of heaven and the goats of the earth."
"Tell me, Sancho," said the duke, "did you see any he-goat among those goats?"
"No, señor," said Sancho; "but I have heard say that none ever passed the horns of the moon."

They didn't care to ask him anything more about his journey, for they saw he was in the mood to go rambling all over the heavens giving an account of everything that went on there, without having ever stirred from the garden. Such, in short, was the end of the adventure of the Distressed Duenna, which gave the duke and duchess laughing matter not only for the time being but for all their lives, and Sancho something to talk about for ages, if he lived so long. But Don Quixote, coming close to his ear, said to him, "Sancho, since you want us to believe what you saw in heaven, I require you to believe me about what I saw in the cave of Montesinos. I say no more."

title: Part 2, Chapter 42
paragraphs: About the advice Don Quixote gave Sancho Panza before he set out to govern the island, together with other well-considered matters

The duke and duchess were so well pleased with the successful and comical outcome of the adventure of the Distressed One that they resolved to keep the joke going, seeing what a fit subject they had to deal with for making it all pass for reality. So, having laid their plans and given their servants and vassals instructions on how to behave toward Sancho in his governorship of the promised island, the day after Clavileño's flight the duke told Sancho to prepare and get ready to go and be governor, since his islanders were already looking out for him like the showers of May.

Sancho bowed and said, "Ever since I came down from heaven and from the top of it beheld the earth, and saw how little it is, the great desire I had to be a governor has been partly cooled in me. What's grand about being ruler on a grain of mustard seed, or what dignity or authority in governing half a dozen men about as big as hazel nuts? — for, as far as I could see, there were no more on the whole earth. If your lordship would be so good as to give me ever so small a bit of heaven, even no more than half a league, I'd rather have it than the best island in the world."

"Remember, Sancho," said the duke, "I cannot give a bit of heaven, not so much as the breadth of my nail, to anyone; rewards and favours of that sort are reserved for God alone. What I can give I give you, and that is a real, genuine island, compact, well proportioned, and uncommonly fertile and fruitful, where, if you know how to use your opportunities, you may, with the help of the world's riches, gain those of heaven."

"Well then," said Sancho, "let the island come; and I'll try to be such a governor that in spite of scoundrels I'll make it to heaven. And it's not from any craving to leave my own humble condition or better myself, but from the desire to find out what it tastes like to be a governor."

"Once you've tried it, Sancho," said the duke, "you'll be eating your fingers off after the governorship, so sweet a thing is it to command and be obeyed. Depend on it: when your master gets to be emperor (as he will, without a doubt, from the course his affairs are taking), it will be no easy matter to wrest the dignity from him, and he will be sore and sorry at heart for having gone so long without becoming one."
"Señor," said Sancho, "it's my belief it's a good thing to be in command, even if it's only over a drove of cattle."

"May I be buried with you, Sancho," said the duke, "but you know everything. I hope you will make as good a governor as your sagacity promises; and that's all I have to say. Now remember: tomorrow is the day you must set out for the governorship of the island, and this evening they will provide you with the proper attire for the role and everything else required for your departure."
"Let them dress me however they like," said Sancho; "however I'm dressed, I'll be Sancho Panza."

"That's true," said the duke; "but one's dress must suit the office or rank one holds; it wouldn't do for a jurist to dress like a soldier, or a soldier like a priest. You, Sancho, will go partly as a lawyer, partly as a captain; for, on the island I'm giving you, arms are needed as much as letters, and letters as much as arms."

"Of letters I know little," said Sancho, "for I don't even know the ABCs; but it's enough for me to have the Christus in my memory to be a good governor. As for arms, I'll handle the ones they give me until I drop, and then, God help me!"
"With so good a memory," said the duke, "Sancho cannot go wrong in anything."

Here Don Quixote joined them; and learning what had passed, and how soon Sancho was to go to his governorship, with the duke's permission he took him by the hand and retired to his room to give him advice on how to conduct himself in his office. As soon as they had entered the room he closed the door behind him and almost by force made Sancho sit down beside him, and in a quiet tone addressed him as follows: "I give infinite thanks to heaven, friend Sancho, that, before I have had any good luck, fortune has come forward to meet you. I, who counted on my good fortune to discharge the recompense of your services, find myself still waiting for advancement, while you, before the time, and contrary to all reasonable expectation, see yourself blessed with the fulfilment of your desires. Some bribe, beg, solicit, rise early, entreat, persist — without attaining the object of their suit; while another comes along and, without knowing why or wherefore, finds himself invested with the office so many have sued for. Here the common saying applies: 'there is good luck as well as bad luck in suits.' You, who to my mind are beyond all doubt a dullard, without early rising or night watching or taking any trouble, with the mere breath of knight-errantry that has breathed upon you, find yourself, without more ado, governor of an island, as though it were a matter of course. I say this, Sancho, so that you don't attribute the favour you have received to your own merits, but give thanks first to heaven that disposes matters beneficently, and second to the great power the profession of knight-errantry contains in itself. With a heart, then, inclined to believe what I have said to you, attend, my son, to your Cato here, who would counsel you and be your polestar and guide to direct and pilot you to a safe haven out of this stormy sea you are about to engulf yourself in; for offices and great trusts are nothing else but a mighty gulf of troubles.
"First of all, my son, you must fear God; for in the fear of him is wisdom, and being wise you cannot err in anything.

"Secondly, you must keep in view what you are, striving to know yourself — the most difficult thing to know that the mind can imagine. If you know yourself, it will follow that you will not puff yourself up like the frog that tried to make himself as large as the ox; if you do, the recollection of having kept pigs in your own country will serve as the ugly feet for the wheel of your folly."

"That's the truth," said Sancho. "But that was when I was a boy; afterwards, when I was a bit more of a man, it was geese I kept, not pigs. But to my mind that has nothing to do with it; not all governors come of kingly stock."

"True," said Don Quixote, "and for that reason, those who are not of noble origin should take care that the dignity of the office they hold is accompanied by a gentle suavity which, wisely managed, will save them from the sneers of malice that no station escapes.

"Glory in your humble birth, Sancho, and don't be ashamed of saying you are peasant-born; for when it's seen you aren't ashamed, no one will set out to put you to the blush. Pride yourself rather on being one of lowly virtue than a lofty sinner. Countless are they who, born of mean parentage, have risen to the highest dignities, pontifical and imperial; of the truth of this I could give you instances enough to weary you.

"Remember, Sancho, if you make virtue your aim and take pride in doing virtuous deeds, you will have no cause to envy those who have princely and lordly ones; for blood is an inheritance, but virtue an acquisition, and virtue has in itself alone a worth that blood does not possess.

"This being so, if perchance any of your kinfolk should come to see you when you are on your island, you are not to repel or slight him, but on the contrary to welcome him, entertain him, and make much of him; for in so doing you will be approved of heaven (which is not pleased that any should despise what it has made), and will comply with the laws of well-ordered nature.

"If you bring your wife with you (and it is not well for those who administer governments to be long without their wives), teach and instruct her, and strive to smooth down her natural roughness; for all that may be gained by a wise governor may be lost and wasted by a boorish, stupid wife.

"If perchance you are left a widower — a thing that may happen — and by virtue of your office seek a consort of higher degree, choose not one to serve you for a hook, or a fishing-rod, or the hood of your 'won't have it'; for truly, I tell you, for all the judge's wife receives, the husband will be held accountable at the general calling to account, where in death he will be made to repay fourfold items that in life he regarded as nothing.
"Never go by arbitrary law, which is so much favoured by ignorant men who plume themselves on cleverness.
"Let the tears of the poor man find with you more compassion, but not more justice, than the pleadings of the rich.
"Strive to lay bare the truth, both amid the promises and presents of the rich man and amid the sobs and entreaties of the poor.
"When equity may and should be brought into play, do not press the utmost rigour of the law against the guilty; for the reputation of the stern judge stands no higher than that of the compassionate.
"If you ever let the staff of justice swerve, let it be not by the weight of a gift, but by that of mercy.
"If it should happen that you must give judgment in the case of one who is your enemy, turn your thoughts away from your own injury and fix them on the justice of the case.

"Let not your own passion blind you in another man's cause; for the errors you will commit that way will most often be irremediable, or if not, only to be remedied at the expense of your good name and even your fortune.

"If any handsome woman comes to seek justice from you, turn your eyes away from her tears and your ears from her lamentations, and consider deliberately the merits of her demand, unless you want your reason swept away by her weeping and your rectitude by her sighs.
"Do not abuse with words the man you have to punish in deed; for the pain of punishment is enough for the unfortunate, without the addition of your scoldings.

"Bear in mind that the culprit who comes under your jurisdiction is but a miserable man subject to all the propensities of our depraved nature; so far as is in your power, show yourself lenient and forbearing; for though the attributes of God are all equal, to our eyes that of mercy is brighter and loftier than that of justice.

"If you follow these precepts and rules, Sancho, your days will be long, your fame eternal, your reward abundant, your felicity unutterable; you will marry your children as you wish, they and your grandchildren will bear titles, you will live in peace and harmony with all men; and when life draws to a close, death will come to you in calm and ripe old age, and the light and loving hands of your great-grandchildren will close your eyes.
"What I have so far addressed to you are instructions for the adornment of your mind. Listen now to those which concern the adornment of your body."

title: Part 2, Chapter 43
paragraphs: About the second set of counsels Don Quixote gave Sancho Panza

Who, hearing the foregoing discourse of Don Quixote, would not have set him down for a person of great good sense and even greater rectitude of purpose? But, as has often been observed in the course of this great history, he only talked nonsense when he touched on chivalry; on every other subject he showed himself to have a clear and unbiased understanding. So at every turn his acts gave the lie to his intellect, and his intellect to his acts. But in this second set of counsels he gave Sancho, he showed himself to have a lively turn of humour, and put both his wisdom and his folly on conspicuous display.

Sancho listened to him with the deepest attention, and tried to fix his counsels in his memory, like one who meant to follow them and by their means bring the full promise of his governorship to a happy issue. Don Quixote, then, went on:

"As to the way you should govern your person and your house, Sancho, the first charge I have to give you is to be clean, and to cut your nails — not letting them grow as some do, whose ignorance makes them fancy that long nails are an ornament to their hands, as if those excrescences they neglect to cut were nails and not the talons of a lizard-catching kestrel — a filthy and unnatural abuse.

"Don't go ungirt and slovenly, Sancho; disordered attire is a sign of an unstable mind, unless the slovenliness and slackness is to be set down to craftiness, as was the common opinion in the case of Julius Caesar.

"Find out cautiously what your office may be worth, and if it allows you to give liveries to your servants, give them respectable and serviceable, rather than showy and gay; and divide them between your servants and the poor. That is to say, if you can clothe six pages, clothe three pages and three poor men, and so you'll have pages for heaven and pages for earth. The vainglorious never think of this new way of giving liveries.

"Don't eat garlic or onions, for fear they find out your peasant origin by the smell. Walk slowly and speak deliberately, but not in such a way as to make it seem you're listening to yourself, for all affectation is bad.
"Dine sparingly and sup more sparingly still; for the health of the whole body is forged in the workshop of the stomach.
"Be temperate in drinking, bearing in mind that wine in excess keeps neither secrets nor promises.
"Take care, Sancho, not to chew on both sides at once, and not to _eruct_ in anyone's presence."
"Eruct!" said Sancho. "I don't know what that means."

"To eruct, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "means to belch — one of the filthiest words in the Spanish language, though a very expressive one. And therefore the genteel have had recourse to the Latin, and instead of 'belch' say 'eruct,' and instead of 'belches' say 'eructations'; and if some don't understand these terms, it matters little, for custom will bring them into use in the course of time, so that they'll be readily understood. This is how a language is enriched; custom and the public are all-powerful in such matters."
"In truth, señor," said Sancho, "one of the counsels and cautions I mean to bear in mind shall be this — not to belch — for I'm constantly doing it."
"Eruct, Sancho, not belch," said Don Quixote.
"Eruct I shall say from now on, and I swear not to forget it," said Sancho.

"Likewise, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "you must not mingle such a quantity of proverbs in your speech as you do; for though proverbs are short maxims, you drag them in so often by the head and shoulders that they smack more of nonsense than of wisdom."

"God alone can cure that," said Sancho. "I have more proverbs in me than a book, and when I speak they come crowding so thick into my mouth that they fall to fighting among themselves to get out. That's why my tongue lets fly the first that come, even if they aren't pat to the purpose. But I'll take care from now on to use only those that befit the dignity of my office; for 'in a house where there's plenty, supper is soon cooked,' and 'he who binds does not wrangle,' and 'the bell-ringer's in a safe berth,' and 'giving and keeping require brains.'"

"That's it, Sancho!" said Don Quixote. "Pack, tack, string proverbs together; nobody's stopping you! 'My mother beats me, and I go on with my tricks.' I'm telling you to avoid proverbs, and here in a second you've shot out a whole litany of them, which have as much to do with what we're talking about as 'over the hills of Úbeda.' Mind, Sancho, I don't say that a proverb aptly brought in is objectionable; but to pile up and string together proverbs at random makes conversation dull and vulgar.

"When you ride on horseback, don't go lolling with your body on the back of the saddle, nor carry your legs stiff or sticking out from the horse's belly, nor yet sit so loosely that one would suppose you were on Dapple; for the seat on a horse makes gentlemen of some and grooms of others.

"Be moderate in your sleep; he who doesn't rise early doesn't get the benefit of the day. And remember, Sancho, diligence is the mother of good fortune, and indolence, its opposite, has never yet attained the object of an honest ambition.

"The last counsel I'll give you now, though it doesn't tend to bodily improvement, I want you to carry carefully in your memory, for I believe it will be no less useful to you than those I've already given. It is this: never engage in a dispute about families, at least in the way of comparing one with another; for necessarily one of those compared will be better than the other, and you will be hated by the one you have disparaged, and get nothing in any shape from the one you have exalted.
"Your attire shall be hose of full length, a long jerkin, and a cloak a trifle longer; loose breeches by no means, for they are becoming neither to gentlemen nor to governors.

"For the present, Sancho, this is all that has occurred to me to advise you; as time goes by and occasions arise, my instructions will follow, if you take care to let me know how you are circumstanced."

"Señor," said Sancho, "I see well enough that all these things your worship has said to me are good, holy, and profitable; but what use will they be to me if I don't remember one of them? To be sure, the bit about not letting my nails grow, and marrying again if I have the chance, won't slip out of my head; but all that other hash, muddle, and jumble — I can't recollect any more of it than of last year's clouds. So it must be given to me in writing; for though I can neither read nor write, I'll give it to my confessor, to drive it into me and remind me of it whenever necessary."

"Ah, sinner that I am!" said Don Quixote. "How bad it looks in governors not to know how to read or write! Let me tell you, Sancho, when a man doesn't know how to read, or is left-handed, it argues one of two things: either that he was the son of exceedingly mean and lowly parents, or that he himself was so incorrigible and ill-conditioned that neither good company nor good teaching could make any impression on him. It is a great defect you labour under, and therefore I would have you learn at any rate to sign your name."

"I can sign my name well enough," said Sancho. "When I was steward of the brotherhood in my village, I learned to make certain letters, like the marks on bales of goods, which they told me made out my name. Besides, I can pretend my right hand is disabled and make someone else sign for me; for 'there's a remedy for everything except death,' and as I'll be in command and hold the staff, I can do as I like. Moreover, 'he who has the alcalde for his father —' and I'll be governor, and that's higher than alcalde. Only come and see! Let them make light of me and abuse me; 'they'll come for wool and go back shorn,' 'whom God loves, his house is known to him,' 'the silly sayings of the rich pass for sayings in the world,' and as I'll be rich, being a governor, and at the same time generous, as I mean to be, no fault will be seen in me. 'Only make yourself honey and the flies will suck you'; 'as much as you have, so much you are worth,' as my grandmother used to say; and 'there's no taking revenge on a man of substance.'"

"Oh, God's curse on you, Sancho!" exclaimed Don Quixote at this. "Sixty thousand devils fly away with you and your proverbs! For the last hour you've been stringing them together and inflicting the pangs of torture on me with every one of them. Those proverbs will bring you to the gallows one day, I promise you; your subjects will take the government from you, or there will be revolts among them. Tell me, where do you pick them up, you booby? How do you apply them, you blockhead? For with me, to utter one and make it apply properly, I have to sweat and labour as if I were digging."

"By God, master mine," said Sancho, "your worship is making a fuss over very little. Why the devil should you be vexed if I make use of what is my own? I have got nothing else, no other stock-in-trade except proverbs and more proverbs. And here are three just this instant come into my head, pat to the purpose and like pears in a basket; but I won't repeat them, for 'sage silence is called Sancho.'"

"That, Sancho, you are not," said Don Quixote; "for not only are you not sage silence, but you are pestilent prate and perversity. Still, I'd like to know what three proverbs have just now come into your memory; for I've been turning over my own — and it is a good one — and none occurs to me."

"What can be better," said Sancho, "than 'never put your thumbs between two back teeth,' and 'to _get out of my house_ and _what do you want with my wife?_ there is no answer,' and 'whether the pitcher hits the stone or the stone the pitcher, it's a bad business for the pitcher'? All of which fit to a hair. For no one should quarrel with his governor, or him in authority over him, because he'll come off worse, as does the man who puts his finger between two back — and even if they're not back teeth, it makes no difference, so long as they're teeth. And to whatever the governor may say, there's no answer, any more than to 'get out of my house' and 'what do you want with my wife?' And as for the stone and the pitcher, a blind man could see that. So 'he who sees the mote in another's eye had better see the beam in his own,' lest it be said of himself, 'the dead woman was frightened by the one with her throat cut'; and your worship knows well that 'the fool knows more in his own house than the wise man in another's.'"

"No, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "the fool knows nothing, either in his own house or anybody else's, for no wise structure of any sort can stand on a foundation of folly. But let's say no more about it, Sancho; if you govern badly, the fault will be yours and the shame mine. I comfort myself with having done my duty in advising you as earnestly and as wisely as I could, and so I am released from my obligations and my promise. God guide you, Sancho, and govern you in your government, and deliver me from the misgiving I have that you will turn the whole island upside down — a thing I might easily prevent by explaining to the duke what you are, and telling him that all that fat little person of yours is nothing else but a sack full of proverbs and sauciness."

"Señor," said Sancho, "if your worship thinks I'm not fit for this governorship, I give it up on the spot; for the mere black of the nail of my soul is dearer to me than my whole body. I can live just as well, simple Sancho, on bread and onions, as I can governor, on partridges and capons. And what's more, while we're asleep we're all equal, great and small, rich and poor. But if your worship looks into it, you'll see it was your worship alone who put me on to this business of governing — for I know no more about the government of islands than a buzzard. And if there's any reason to think that because of my being governor the devil will get hold of me, I'd rather go Sancho to heaven than governor to hell."

"By God, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "for those last words you have uttered alone, I consider you deserve to be governor of a thousand islands. You have good natural instincts, without which no knowledge is worth anything. Commend yourself to God, and try not to swerve in the pursuit of your main object; I mean, always make it your aim and fixed purpose to do right in all matters that come before you, for heaven always helps good intentions. And now let's go to dinner, for I think my lord and lady are waiting for us."

title: Part 2, Chapter 44
paragraphs: How Sancho Panza was conducted to his governorship, and of the strange adventure that befell Don Quixote in the castle
