It is stated, they say, in the true original of this history, that when Cide Hamete came to write this chapter, his interpreter did not translate it as he wrote it — that is, as a kind of complaint the Moor made against himself for having taken in hand a story so dry and of so little variety as this of Don Quixote, for he found himself forced to speak perpetually of him and Sancho, without venturing to indulge in digressions and episodes more serious and more interesting. He said, too, that to go on always with mind, hand, and pen restricted to a single subject, and speaking through the mouths of a few characters, was intolerable drudgery, the result of which was never equal to the author's labour. To avoid this, in the First Part he had availed himself of the device of novellas, like "The Ill-advised Curiosity" and "The Captive Captain," which stand, as it were, apart from the story; the others given there are incidents that happened to Don Quixote himself and could not be omitted. He also thought, he says, that many readers, engrossed by the interest of Don Quixote's exploits, would take no interest in the novellas, and would skim them hastily or impatiently without noticing the elegance and art of their composition — qualities which would be very clear if they had been published on their own and not as mere appendages to the crazes of Don Quixote or the simplicities of Sancho. Therefore, in this Second Part he thought it best not to insert novellas, either separate or interwoven, but only episodes, something like them, arising from the circumstances the facts present; and even these sparingly, with no more words than suffice to make them plain. Confining and restricting himself to the narrow limits of the narrative, though he has ability, capacity, and brains enough to deal with the whole universe, he requests that his labours not be despised, and that credit be given him not only for what he writes but for what he has refrained from writing.

And so he goes on with his story, saying that on the day Don Quixote gave his counsels to Sancho, the same afternoon after dinner he handed them to him in writing so that he could get someone to read them to him. They had scarcely been handed over, however, when he let them drop, and they fell into the hands of the duke, who showed them to the duchess; and both were amazed once again at the madness and wit of Don Quixote. To carry on the joke, then, the same evening they dispatched Sancho with a large following to the village that was to serve as his island. It happened that the man in charge of him was a majordomo of the duke's, a man of great discretion and humour — and there can be no humour without discretion — and the same one who had played the part of Countess Trifaldi in the comical way already described. Thus qualified, and instructed by his master and mistress on how to deal with Sancho, he carried out their scheme admirably. Now it came to pass that as soon as Sancho saw this majordomo, he seemed to recognise in his features those of the Trifaldi; and turning to his master, he said, "Señor, either the devil will carry me off here on this spot, righteous and believing, or your worship will admit to me that the face of this majordomo of the duke's is the very face of the Distressed One."

Don Quixote looked attentively at the majordomo, and having done so, said to Sancho, "There is no reason why the devil should carry you off, Sancho, either righteous or believing — and what you mean by that I don't know. The face of the Distressed One is the face of the majordomo, but for all that, the majordomo is not the Distressed One; his being so would involve a mighty contradiction. But this is not the time for going into questions of the sort, which would involve us in an inextricable labyrinth. Believe me, my friend, we must pray earnestly to our Lord that he deliver us both from wicked wizards and enchanters."

"It's no joke, señor," said Sancho. "Before this I heard him speak, and it was exactly as if the voice of the Trifaldi was sounding in my ears. Well, I'll hold my peace, but I'll take care to be on the lookout from now on for any sign that might confirm or do away with this suspicion."
"You will do well, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and you will let me know everything you discover, and everything that happens to you in your governorship."

Sancho at last set out, attended by a great number of people. He was dressed in the garb of a lawyer, with a tawny watered camlet gaban over everything and a montera cap of the same material, and mounted _a la jineta_ on a mule. Behind him, in accordance with the duke's orders, followed Dapple with brand-new ass-trappings and silk ornaments; and from time to time Sancho turned around to look at his ass, so pleased to have him along that he wouldn't have traded places with the emperor of Germany. On taking leave he kissed the hands of the duke and duchess and received his master's blessing, which Don Quixote gave him in tears, while Sancho received it blubbering.

Let worthy Sancho go in peace, and good luck to him, Gentle Reader; and look forward to two bushels of laughter from the account of how he conducted himself in office. In the meantime, turn your attention to what happened to his master that same night; and if you don't laugh at it, at any rate you will stretch your mouth in a grin, for Don Quixote's adventures must be honoured either with wonder or with laughter.

It is recorded, then, that as soon as Sancho was gone, Don Quixote felt his loneliness, and had it been possible for him to revoke the mandate and take the governorship away from him, he would have done so. The duchess noticed his dejection and asked him why he was melancholy; because, she said, if it was for the loss of Sancho, there were squires, duennas, and damsels in her house who would wait upon him to his full satisfaction.

"The truth is, señora," replied Don Quixote, "that I do feel the loss of Sancho; but that is not the main cause of my looking sad. And of all the offers your excellency makes me, I accept only the goodwill with which they are made; as for the rest, I entreat your excellency to permit me to wait upon myself alone in my chamber."
"Indeed, Señor Don Quixote," said the duchess, "that must not be; four of my damsels, as beautiful as flowers, shall wait upon you."

"To me," said Don Quixote, "they will not be flowers, but thorns to pierce my heart. They, or anything like them, shall as soon enter my chamber as fly. If your highness wishes to gratify me still further, though I deserve it not, permit me to please myself and wait upon myself in my own room; for I place a barrier between my inclinations and my virtue, and I do not wish to break this rule through the generosity your highness is disposed to display toward me. In short, I would rather sleep in my clothes than let anyone undress me."

"Say no more, Señor Don Quixote, say no more," said the duchess. "I assure you I will give orders that not even a fly, let alone a damsel, shall enter your room. I am not the one to undermine the propriety of Señor Don Quixote, for it strikes me that among his many virtues the one most pre-eminent is that of modesty. Your worship may undress and dress in private and in your own way, as you please and when you please, for there will be no one to hinder you; and in your chamber you will find all the utensils required to supply the wants of one who sleeps with his door locked, so that no natural needs compel you to open it. May the great Dulcinea del Toboso live a thousand years, and may her fame extend across the whole surface of the globe, for she deserves to be loved by a knight so valiant and so virtuous; and may kind heaven infuse zeal into the heart of our governor Sancho Panza to finish off his discipline speedily, so that the world may once more enjoy the beauty of so grand a lady."

To which Don Quixote replied, "Your highness has spoken like what you are; from the mouth of a noble lady nothing bad can come; and Dulcinea will be more fortunate, and better known to the world by the praise of your highness, than by all the eulogies the greatest orators on earth could bestow upon her."

"Well, well, Señor Don Quixote," said the duchess, "it is nearly supper-time, and the duke is probably waiting. Come, let us go to supper, and retire to rest early; for the journey you made yesterday from Kandy was not so short that it must not have caused you some fatigue."

"I feel none, señora," said Don Quixote. "I'd go so far as to swear to your excellency that in all my life I never mounted a quieter beast, or a pleasanter-paced one, than Clavileño; and I don't know what could have induced Malambruno to discard a steed so swift and so gentle, and burn it so recklessly as he did."

"Probably," said the duchess, "repenting of the evil he had done to the Trifaldi and her company, and to others, and of the crimes he must have committed as a wizard and enchanter, he resolved to make away with all the instruments of his craft; and so he burned Clavileño as the chief one, and the one that mainly kept him restless, wandering from land to land. By its ashes and by the trophy of the placard, the valour of the great Don Quixote of La Mancha is established forever."

Don Quixote renewed his thanks to the duchess; and having supped, retired to his chamber alone, refusing to allow anyone to enter with him to wait on him, such was his fear of encountering temptations that might lead or drive him to forget his chaste fidelity to his lady Dulcinea — for he always had present to his mind the virtue of Amadis, that flower and mirror of knights-errant. He locked the door behind him, and by the light of two wax candles he undressed himself; but as he was taking off his stockings — O disaster unworthy of such a personage! — there came a burst, not of sighs, nor anything that might belie his delicacy or good breeding, but of some two dozen stitches in one of his stockings, which made it look like a window-lattice. The worthy gentleman was beyond measure distressed, and at that moment he would have given an ounce of silver to have half a drachm of green silk on hand; I say green silk because the stockings were green.

Here Cide Hamete exclaimed as he was writing, "O poverty, poverty! I don't know what could have possessed the great Cordovan poet to call you 'holy gift ungratefully received.' Although a Moor, I know well enough from my dealings with Christians that holiness consists in charity, humility, faith, obedience, and poverty; but for all that, I say he must have a great deal of godliness who can find any satisfaction in being poor — unless, indeed, it be the kind of poverty one of their greatest saints refers to, saying, 'possess all things as though you possessed them not,' which is what they call poverty in spirit. But you, that other poverty — for it is of you I am speaking now — why do you love to fall out with gentlemen and men of good birth more than with other people? Why do you compel them to smear over the cracks in their shoes, and to have the buttons on their coats one of silk, another of hair, and another of glass? Why must their ruffs be always crinkled like endive leaves and not crimped with a crimping iron?" (From this we may see the antiquity of starch and crimped ruffs.) Then he goes on: "Poor gentleman of good family! Always cockering up his honour, dining miserably and in secret, and making a hypocrite of the toothpick with which he sallies out into the street after eating nothing to oblige him to use it! Poor fellow, I say, with his nervous honour, fancying they perceive a league off the patch on his shoe, the sweat-stains on his hat, the shabbiness of his cloak, and the hunger in his stomach!"

All this was brought home to Don Quixote by the bursting of his stitches; however, he comforted himself on noticing that Sancho had left behind a pair of travelling boots, which he resolved to wear the next day. At last he went to bed, low in spirits and heavy at heart, as much because he missed Sancho as because of the irreparable disaster to his stockings, the stitches of which he would even have taken up with silk of another colour — one of the greatest signs of poverty a gentleman can show in the course of his never-failing embarrassments. He put out the candles; but the night was warm and he could not sleep. He rose from his bed and opened slightly a grated window that looked out on a beautiful garden, and as he did so he heard people walking and talking in the garden below. He listened attentively, and those below raised their voices so that he could hear these words:

"Don't urge me to sing, Emerencia; you know that ever since this stranger entered the castle and my eyes beheld him, I can't sing — only weep. Besides, my lady is a light rather than a heavy sleeper, and I wouldn't for all the wealth of the world have her find us here. And even if she were asleep and didn't wake, my singing would be in vain, if this strange Aeneas, who has come into my neighbourhood to flout me, sleeps on and doesn't wake to hear it."

"Don't worry about that, dear Altisidora," replied a voice. "The duchess is no doubt asleep, and everyone in the house except the lord of your heart and disturber of your soul; for just now I saw him open the grated window of his chamber, so he must be awake. Sing, my poor sufferer, in a low sweet tone to the accompaniment of your harp; and even if the duchess hears us, we can lay the blame on the heat of the night."

"That is not the point, Emerencia," replied Altisidora; "it is that I would not have my singing lay bare my heart, and have me thought a light and wanton maiden by those who do not know the mighty power of love. But come what may; better a blush on the cheeks than a sore in the heart." And here a harp, softly touched, made itself heard. As Don Quixote listened to all this, he was in a state of breathless amazement, for instantly the countless adventures like this — with windows, gratings, gardens, serenades, lovemakings, and languishings — that he had read of in his trashy books of chivalry, came to mind. He at once concluded that some damsel of the duchess's was in love with him, and that her modesty forced her to keep her passion secret. He trembled lest he should fall, and made an inward resolution not to yield; and commending himself with all his might and soul to his lady Dulcinea, he made up his mind to listen to the music. To let them know he was there, he gave a pretended sneeze, at which the damsels were not a little delighted, for all they wanted was that Don Quixote should hear them. So having tuned the harp, Altisidora, running her hand across the strings, began this ballad:
O you who lie above in bed, / Between the holland sheets, / Stretched out from night till morn, / With outstretched legs asleep;
O you, most valiant knight of all / The famed Manchegan breed, / Of purity and virtue more / Than gold of Araby;
Give ear unto a suffering maid, / Well-grown but evil-starred, / For those two suns of yours have lit / A fire within her heart.
Adventures seeking you do rove, / To others bringing woe; / You scatter wounds, but ah, the balm / To heal them you withhold!
Say, valiant youth, and so may God / Your enterprises speed, / Did you the light mid Libya's sands / Or Jaca's rocks first see?
Did scaly serpents give you suck? / Who nursed you when a babe? / Were you cradled in the forest rude, / Or gloomy mountain cave?
O Dulcinea may be proud, / That plump and lusty maid; / For she alone has had the power / A tiger fierce to tame.
And she for this shall famous be / From Tagus to Jarama, / From Manzanares to Genil, / From Duero to Arlanza.
Fain would I change with her, and give / A petticoat to boot, / The best and bravest that I have, / All trimmed with gold galloon.
O to be the happy fair / Your mighty arms enfold, / Or even sit beside your bed / And scratch your dusty poll!
I rave, — to favours such as these / Unworthy to aspire; / Your feet to tickle were enough / For one so mean as I.
What caps, what slippers silver-laced, / Would I on you bestow! / What damask breeches make for you; / What fine long holland cloaks!
And I would give you pearls that should / As big as oak-galls show; / So matchless big that each might well / Be called the great "Alone."
Manchegan Nero, look not down / From your Tarpeian Rock / Upon this burning heart, nor add / The fuel of your wrath.
A virgin soft and young am I, / Not yet fifteen years old; / (I'm only three months past fourteen, / I swear upon my soul).
I hobble not nor do I limp, / All blemish I'm without, / And as I walk my lily locks / Are trailing on the ground.
And though my nose be rather flat, / And though my mouth be wide, / My teeth like topazes exalt / My beauty to the sky.
You know that my voice is sweet, / That is if you do hear; / And I am moulded in a form / Somewhat below the mean.
These charms, and many more, are yours, / Spoils to your spear and bow; / A damsel of this house am I, / By name Altisidora.

Here the song of the heart-stricken Altisidora came to an end, while the warmly wooed Don Quixote began to feel alarmed; and with a deep sigh he said to himself, "O that I should be such an unlucky knight that no damsel can set eyes on me without falling in love with me! O that the peerless Dulcinea should be so unfortunate that they cannot let her enjoy my incomparable constancy in peace! What would you have with her, you queens? Why do you persecute her, you empresses? Why do you pursue her, you virgins of from fourteen to fifteen? Leave the unhappy being to triumph, rejoice, and glory in the lot love has been pleased to bestow upon her in surrendering my heart and yielding up my soul to her. You love-smitten host, know that to Dulcinea alone I am dough and sugar-paste, flint to all others; for her I am honey, for you aloes. For me Dulcinea alone is beautiful, wise, virtuous, graceful, and high-bred, and all others are ill-favoured, foolish, light, and low-born. Nature sent me into the world to be hers and no other's. Altisidora may weep or sing, the lady for whose sake they belaboured me in the castle of the enchanted Moor may give way to despair, but I must be Dulcinea's, boiled or roast, pure, courteous, and chaste, in spite of all the magic-working powers on earth." And with that he shut the window with a bang, and, as much out of temper and out of sorts as if some great misfortune had befallen him, stretched himself on his bed, where we will leave him for the present, as the great Sancho Panza, who is about to set up his famous governorship, now demands our attention.

title: Part 2, Chapter 45
paragraphs: How the great Sancho Panza took possession of his island, and how he began to govern

O perpetual discoverer of the antipodes, torch of the world, eye of heaven, sweet rocker of the water-jars! Thimbraeus in one place, Phœbus in another, archer at one moment, healer the next, father of poetry, inventor of music; you who always rise and, whatever it may look like, never set! To you, O Sun, by whose help man begets man — to you I appeal: assist me, and brighten the darkness of my wits, so that I can proceed with scrupulous accuracy in recounting the government of the great Sancho Panza; for without you I feel weak, faint, and unsure of myself.

To get to the point, then: Sancho, with his whole retinue, arrived at a village of about a thousand inhabitants, one of the largest the duke owned. They told him it was called the island of Barataria — either because the village's name was Baratario, or because of the joke by which the governorship had been handed to him. When he reached the gates of the town, which was walled, the town council came out to meet him, the bells pealed, the inhabitants displayed every sign of general delight, and with great pomp they escorted him to the principal church to give thanks to God. Then, with mock ceremonies, they presented him with the keys of the town and acknowledged him as perpetual governor of the island of Barataria. The clothes, the beard, and the short, fat figure of the new governor astonished everyone who was not in on the secret — and even everyone who was, and they were not few. Finally, leading him out of the church, they brought him to the judgment seat and installed him on it, and the duke's majordomo said to him, "It is an ancient custom on this island, señor governor, that whoever comes to take possession of this famous island must answer a question put to him — one that has to be somewhat tangled and difficult. From his answer the people take the measure of their new governor's intelligence, and either rejoice at his arrival or lament it accordingly."

While the majordomo was delivering this speech, Sancho was staring at some large letters inscribed on the wall facing his seat, and since he could not read, he asked what that painted writing on the wall was. The answer came: "Señor, the day on which your lordship took possession of this island is written and recorded there, and the inscription reads: 'On this day, the such-and-such of such-and-such a month and year, Señor Don Sancho Panza took possession of this island; may he enjoy it for many years.'"
"And who is it they're calling Don Sancho Panza?" asked Sancho.
"Your lordship," replied the majordomo, "for no Panza other than the one now sitting in that chair has ever set foot on this island."

"Well then, let me tell you something, brother," said Sancho. "I don't have the 'Don,' and nobody in my family has ever had it. My name is plain Sancho Panza; Sancho was my father's name, and Sancho was my grandfather's, and they were all Panzas, with no Dons or Doñas stuck on. I suspect there are more Dons than stones on this island; but no matter — God knows what I mean, and if my government lasts four days, maybe I'll weed out these Dons, which must be as much of a plague as the midges, there are so many of them. Let the majordomo get on with his question, and I'll answer as best I can, whether the people lament or not."

At that moment two old men entered the court, one of them using a cane as a walking-stick, and the one without a stick said, "Señor, some time ago I lent this good man ten gold-crowns in gold, to oblige him and do him a favor, on the understanding that he would return them whenever I asked for them. A long while went by before I did ask, because I didn't want to put him in any tighter spot to repay them than he was in when I lent them. But when it seemed to me he was getting careless about paying, I asked him for them — once, and then several times — and not only will he not give them back, he denies owing them at all. He says I never lent him any such crowns, or that if I did, he repaid them. I have no witnesses to the loan or to the repayment — because he never repaid me. I want your worship to put him on his oath, and if he swears that he returned them to me, I forgive him the debt, here and before God."
"What do you say to this, good old man — you with the stick?" said Sancho.

To which the old man answered, "I admit, señor, that he lent them to me; but let your worship lower your staff, and since he leaves it to my oath, I'll swear that I gave them back and paid him truly and honestly."

The governor lowered the staff, and as he did, the old man with the stick handed it to the other old man to hold for him while he swore, as though it were in his way; he then placed his hand on the cross of the staff and declared that it was true the ten crowns demanded of him had indeed been lent to him, but that he had, with his own hand, returned them into the other man's hand, and that the other, failing to remember it, kept asking for them over and over.

Seeing this, the great governor asked the creditor what reply he had to make to his opponent's statement. He said that his debtor had no doubt told the truth, for he held him to be an honest man and a good Christian; he himself must have forgotten when and how the crowns had been given back to him, and from then on he would never demand them of him again.

The debtor picked up his stick again, bowed his head, and left the court. Sancho, watching this — how he simply walked off without another word — and noting the plaintiff's resignation, dropped his head onto his chest and stayed for a little while deep in thought, the forefinger of his right hand pressed against his brow and nose; then he lifted his head and ordered them to call back the old man with the stick, who had already gone. They brought him back, and the moment Sancho saw him he said, "Honest man, give me that stick — I need it."
"Gladly," said the old man; "here it is, señor," and he placed it in his hand.
Sancho took it, handed it to the other old man, and said to him, "Go, and God go with you — you are paid now."
"Paid — I, señor?" returned the old man. "What, is this cane worth ten gold-crowns?"

"Yes," said the governor, "or if it isn't, I'm the biggest blockhead alive. Now you'll all see whether I have the head to govern an entire kingdom." And he ordered the cane to be broken in two, right there in front of everyone. It was done, and inside it they found ten gold-crowns. Everyone was stunned, and they took their governor for a second Solomon. They asked him how he had worked out that the ten crowns were inside the cane, and he answered: he had noticed that the old man who took the oath handed his stick to his opponent while he was swearing, and swore that he had truly and honestly given him the crowns — and that the instant he finished swearing, he asked for the stick back. From this it had occurred to him that the sum being demanded must be inside it. And from this, he said, one could see that God sometimes guides the judgments of those who govern, even when they are fools; besides, he had heard the curate of his village tell of a case exactly like it, and his memory was so good that, if he didn't forget everything he wanted to remember, there wouldn't be a memory like his on the whole island. In the end the two old men departed, one humiliated and the other thoroughly satisfied; everyone present was astonished; and the man whose job it was to record Sancho's words, deeds, and movements could not decide whether to write him down as a fool or as a man of sense.

No sooner was this case settled than a woman came into court, gripping tightly onto a man dressed like a prosperous cattle dealer. She came forward shouting at the top of her voice, "Justice, señor governor, justice! And if I don't find it on earth, I'll go looking for it in heaven! Señor governor of my soul, this wicked man caught me out in the middle of the fields and used my body as if it were a badly washed rag, and — wretched me! — he took from me what I had guarded for more than twenty-three years, defending it against Moors and Christians, locals and strangers alike. I've always been as hard as an oak, keeping myself as pure as a salamander in the fire or wool among the brambles — and now this fine fellow comes along with clean hands to lay them on me!"
"Whether this gallant's hands are clean or not is still to be proved," said Sancho; and turning to the man, he asked him what he had to say in reply to the woman's accusation.

Thoroughly flustered, the man answered, "Sirs, I'm a poor pig dealer, and this morning I left the village to sell — begging your pardon — four pigs, and between taxes and swindles they took from me little less than what the pigs were worth. As I was heading back to my village, I met this good lady on the road, and the devil, who tangles and spoils everything, yoked us together. I paid her properly, but she wasn't satisfied; she grabbed hold of me and never let go until she'd dragged me here. She says I forced her, but she's lying, by the oath I swear or am ready to swear; and that's the whole truth, down to the last crumb of it."

At this the governor asked him whether he had any silver money on him; he said he had about twenty ducats in a leather purse inside his shirt. The governor ordered him to take it out and hand it over to the complainant; trembling, he obeyed. The woman took it, and after bowing a thousand times to everyone and praying God for the long life and health of the señor governor, who looked after needy orphans and maidens so well, she hurried out of court clutching the purse in both hands — though not before checking whether the money inside it was really silver.

The moment she was gone, Sancho said to the cattle dealer, whose tears were already welling up and whose eyes and heart were trailing after his purse, "Good fellow, go after that woman and take the purse from her — by force if you have to — and bring it back here." And he was not speaking to a fool or a deaf man, for the fellow shot off like a bolt of lightning to do as he was told.

All the bystanders waited in suspense to see how the case would end, and before long the man and the woman returned, locked together even more tightly than before — she with her skirt hitched up and the purse cradled in the lap of it, he straining with all his might to wrench it from her, but utterly in vain, so fierce was the woman's defense. All the while she kept screaming, "Justice from God and from the world! Look here, señor governor, at the shamelessness and gall of this villain, who in the middle of town, in the middle of the street, tried to snatch from me the purse your worship ordered him to give me!"
"And did he get it?" asked the governor.

"Get it!" said the woman. "I'd sooner let him take my life than the purse. A fine baby I'd be! They'll have to throw a different sort of cat in my face than this miserable, mangy wretch. Pincers and hammers, mallets and chisels couldn't pry it out of my grip — no, nor a lion's claws; they'd have the soul out of my body first!"
"She's right," said the man. "I give up — I'm beaten and helpless. I confess I haven't the strength to take it from her." And he let go of her.

At this the governor said to the woman, "Show me that purse, my worthy and valiant friend." She handed it over at once, and the governor returned it to the man and said to the unforced mistress of force, "Sister, if you had shown the same spirit and vigor in defending your body that you've just shown in defending that purse — or even half as much — the strength of Hercules himself could not have forced you. Be off with you, and God speed you, and bad luck go with you; and don't show your face anywhere on this island, or within six leagues of it in any direction, on pain of two hundred lashes. Off with you now, I say, you shameless, swindling shrew."

The woman was thoroughly cowed and slunk away dejected, hanging her head; and the governor said to the man, "Honest man, go home with your money, and God go with you; and from now on, if you don't want to lose it, see that you don't get the urge to yoke yourself with anyone." The man thanked him as awkwardly as he knew how and went his way, and the onlookers were once again filled with admiration for their new governor's rulings and sentences.

Next, two men presented themselves before him — one apparently a farm laborer, the other a tailor, for he carried a pair of shears in his hand — and the tailor said, "Señor governor, this laborer and I appear before your worship because yesterday this honest man came into my shop (for, begging everyone's pardon, I'm a certified master tailor, God be thanked), put a piece of cloth into my hands, and asked me, 'Señor, would there be enough in this cloth to make me a cap?' I measured the cloth and told him there would. He must have suspected — as I supposed, and supposed correctly — that I meant to steal some of his cloth, going by his own crookedness and the low opinion people have of tailors; and so he told me to check whether there would be enough for two. I guessed what he was driving at and said 'yes,' and he, still riding his original ungenerous notion, kept adding cap after cap while I added 'yes' after 'yes,' until we reached five. Just now he came to collect them. I handed them over, but he refuses to pay me for the work — instead he demands that I pay him, or give him back his cloth."
"Is all this true, brother?" said Sancho.
"Yes," the man replied; "but will your worship make him show the five caps he's made me?"

"Gladly," said the tailor; and pulling his hand out from under his cloak, he displayed five caps perched on the five fingers of it and said, "There are the caps this good man asks for, and by God and on my conscience I haven't a scrap of cloth left over, and I'll gladly have the work examined by the inspectors of the trade."

Everyone present laughed at the number of caps and the oddity of the lawsuit. Sancho thought it over for a moment and then said, "It strikes me that this case calls for no long-winded arguments, only the snap judgment of an honest man; so my ruling is this: the tailor loses his fee and the laborer his cloth, the caps go to the prisoners in the jail, and let that be the end of it."

If the earlier ruling about the cattle dealer's purse had stirred the bystanders' admiration, this one set them laughing; still, the governor's orders were carried out in the end. All of it, having been written down by his chronicler, was immediately dispatched to the duke, who was awaiting it eagerly. And here let us leave the good Sancho; for his master, deeply shaken by Altisidora's music, has urgent claims on our attention now.

title: Part 2, Chapter 46
paragraphs: Of the terrible fright with bells and cats that Don Quixote suffered in the course of the lovesick Altisidora’s wooing

We left Don Quixote wrapped in the thoughts that the music of the lovesick maiden Altisidora had stirred in him. He carried them to bed with him, and like fleas they gave him no sleep and not a moment’s rest, and the broken stitches of his stockings joined in the torment. But Time is swift and nothing can slow his course, so he came riding along on the hours, and morning soon arrived. Seeing this, Don Quixote abandoned the soft feather bed and, in no way lazy, dressed himself in his chamois suit and pulled on his traveling boots to hide the disaster that had befallen his stockings. Over it all he threw his scarlet cloak, set on his head a montera cap of green velvet trimmed with silver edging, slung across his shoulder the baldric that carried his good keen sword, took up a large rosary he always kept with him, and with great solemnity and a measured stride made his way to the antechamber, where the duke and duchess were already dressed and waiting for him. But as he passed through a gallery, Altisidora and her friend, the other damsel, were lying in wait for him, and the moment Altisidora caught sight of him she pretended to faint, while her friend caught her in her lap and began hurriedly unlacing the bodice of her dress.
Don Quixote saw it, and coming up to them he said, “I know perfectly well what lies behind this fainting fit.”

“I have no idea what causes it,” the friend replied, “for Altisidora is the healthiest damsel in this whole house, and I have never heard so much as a complaint from her in all the time I have known her. A plague on every knight-errant in the world, if they are all so ungrateful! Go away, Señor Don Quixote, for this poor child will not come back to her senses as long as you stay here.”

To which Don Quixote answered, “Do me the favor, señora, of having a lute placed in my chamber tonight, and I will comfort this poor maiden as best I can; for in the early stages of love a swift disillusionment is a remedy of proven worth.” And with that he withdrew, so as not to be noticed by anyone who might see him there.

He had scarcely gone when Altisidora, recovering from her swoon, said to her companion, “The lute must be left for him, for Don Quixote clearly means to give us some music, and since it will be his, it will not be bad.”

They went at once to tell the duchess what was happening and about the lute Don Quixote had asked for, and she, delighted beyond measure, schemed with the duke and her two damsels to play a trick on him that would be amusing but do no harm; and in high spirits they waited for night, which came as quickly as the day had come; and as for the day, the duke and duchess passed it in delightful conversation with Don Quixote.

When eleven o’clock struck, Don Quixote found a guitar in his chamber. He tried it, opened the window, and noticed that people were walking in the garden; and after running his fingers over the frets of the guitar and tuning it as well as he could, he spat and cleared his throat, and then, in a voice a little hoarse but full and rounded, he sang the following ballad, which he himself had composed that very day:

Mighty Love unsettles maidens’ hearts
and throws them into confusion,
and the instrument he favors
above all others is idleness.

Sewing, stitching, any labor,
keeping busy hands at work,
is the surest antidote
to the poison Love pours in.

And for right-minded maidens
who hope to bear a matron’s name,
modesty is their marriage portion,
modesty their highest praise.

Men of prudence and discretion,
merry courtiers and gallant knights,
may dally with the forward damsels,
but they take the modest ones to wife.
There are passions brief and fleeting,
loves declared at wayside inns —
loves that rise with the sunrise
and end when the guest has gone his way.

Love that springs up swift and sudden,
here today, tomorrow flown,
passes on and leaves no trace,
leaves no image on the soul.

A painting laid over a painting
makes no showing of its own;
where one beauty holds possession,
no other beauty can take hold.

Dulcinea del Toboso
is painted on my heart;
never, never from its tablets
can her image be erased.

Of all the virtues in a lover
the one most prized is constancy;
by this love works its wonders,
by this lovers are raised to the skies.

Don Quixote had gotten this far in his song — to which the duke, the duchess, Altisidora, and nearly the whole household of the castle were listening — when suddenly, from a gallery directly above his window, someone let down a cord strung with more than a hundred bells, and right after it emptied out a great sack of cats, each with smaller bells tied to its tail. So great was the clanging of the bells and the yowling of the cats that even the duke and duchess, who had invented the joke, were startled by it, while Don Quixote froze, paralyzed with fear. And as luck would have it, two or three of the cats got in through the grating of his chamber and, tearing from one side of the room to the other, made it seem as if a legion of devils had been let loose inside. They put out the candles burning in the room and raced about looking for some way to escape; the cord with the big bells never stopped rising and falling; and most of the people in the castle, having no idea what was actually going on, were beside themselves with astonishment. Don Quixote sprang to his feet, drew his sword, and began thrusting at the grating, shouting, “Away, malignant enchanters! Away, you spell-weaving rabble! I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, against whom your wicked schemes have no force and no power.” Then, turning on the cats that were racing around the room, he slashed at them again and again. They bolted for the grating and escaped through it — all but one, which, finding itself hard pressed by the strokes of Don Quixote’s sword, flew at his face and fastened onto his nose with teeth and claws, and the pain of it set him roaring at the top of his lungs. Hearing this and guessing the cause, the duke and duchess ran to his room with all speed, and as the poor gentleman strained with all his might to pry the cat off his face, they opened the door with a master key and came in with lights, where they beheld the unequal combat. The duke ran forward to separate the combatants, but Don Quixote shouted, “Let no one take him from me! Leave me hand to hand with this demon, this wizard, this enchanter; I will teach him myself who Don Quixote of La Mancha is.” The cat, however, paid no attention to these threats; it snarled and held on; but at last the duke pulled it loose and flung it out the window. Don Quixote was left with a face as full of holes as a sieve and a nose in none too good a state, and deeply annoyed that they had not let him finish the battle he had been fighting so stoutly against that villain of an enchanter. They sent for some oil of St. John’s wort, and Altisidora herself, with her own fair hands, bandaged every wounded spot; and as she did so she said to him in a low voice, “All these misfortunes have come upon you, hard-hearted knight, for the sin of your coldness and your obstinacy; and God grant your squire Sancho forgets to whip himself, so that this dearly beloved Dulcinea of yours may never be freed from her enchantment, and you may never come to her bed — at least not while I, who adore you, am alive.”

To all this Don Quixote answered nothing but deep sighs, and then he stretched himself out on his bed, thanking the duke and duchess for their kindness — not because he had felt any fear of that bell-ringing rabble of enchanters in cat form, but because he recognized the goodwill they had shown in coming to his rescue. The duke and duchess left him to rest and withdrew, deeply sorry at how badly the joke had turned out, for they had never imagined the adventure would fall so heavily on Don Quixote or cost him so dear: it cost him five days confined to his bed, during which another adventure befell him, a pleasanter one than the last — though his chronicler will not tell it just now, so that he may turn his attention to Sancho Panza, who was carrying on his government with great diligence and great drollery.

title: Part 2, Chapter 47
paragraphs: In which the account continues of how Sancho Panza behaved in his government

The history tells us that they led Sancho from the courtroom to a magnificent palace, where a table had been set with royal splendor in a vast hall. Trumpets blared as Sancho came into the room, and four pages stepped forward offering him water for his hands, which Sancho accepted with great dignity. The music stopped, and Sancho took his seat at the head of the table — the only seat there was, with only a single place laid. A figure who later turned out to be a physician stationed himself standing at Sancho's side, holding a whalebone wand in his hand. Then they lifted away a fine white cloth that had been covering fruit and a wide assortment of dishes of every kind; a man who appeared to be a student said grace, and one page tied a lace-trimmed bib around Sancho's neck while another, acting as head carver, set a plate of fruit in front of him. But he had barely tasted a bite when the man with the wand tapped the plate, and it was whisked away from him with astonishing speed. The carver promptly set another dish before him, and Sancho moved to try it; yet before he could even reach it, let alone taste it, the wand had already touched it and a page carried it off as quickly as the fruit had gone. Watching this, Sancho was bewildered, and glancing around from face to face, he asked whether this dinner was meant to be eaten like a conjurer's sleight-of-hand act.

The man with the wand answered, “It is not to be eaten, señor governor, except in the manner usual and customary on other islands where there are governors. I, señor, am a physician, and I draw a salary on this island to serve its governors in that capacity, and I care far more for their health than for my own. I study day and night, learning the governor's constitution thoroughly so that I can cure him if he falls ill. My principal duty is to be present at his dinners and suppers, permitting him to eat whatever I judge suitable for him and withholding whatever I believe will harm him or injure his stomach. That is why I ordered the plate of fruit taken away, as being too moist, and that other dish removed for being too hot and full of spices that provoke thirst; for the man who drinks too much destroys and burns up the radical moisture in which life itself resides.”
“Well then,” said Sancho, “that dish of roast partridges over there, which looks so appetizing, surely won't do me any harm.”
To this the physician replied, “Of those my lord the governor shall not eat a single one as long as I draw breath.”
“And why not?” said Sancho.

“Because,” the doctor answered, “our master Hippocrates, the polestar and guiding light of medicine, declares in one of his aphorisms _omnis saturatio mala, perdicis autem pessima_, which means ‘all overeating is bad, but overeating partridge is the worst of all.’”

“In that case,” said Sancho, “let the señor doctor look over the dishes on this table and pick out the one that will do me the most good and the least harm, and let me eat it without his tapping it with that stick of his; because by the life of the governor — and God grant I live to enjoy it — I am dying of hunger; and whatever the doctor may say, denying me food is the way to end my life, not to lengthen it.”

“Your worship speaks the truth, señor governor,” said the physician; “and so it is my judgment that your worship should not eat those stewed rabbits over there, since rabbit is a furry sort of food; that veal you might have sampled, if it had not been roasted and served with pickles, but as things stand it is out of the question.”

“That big dish steaming away farther down the table,” said Sancho, “looks to me like an olla podrida, and with the variety of things that go into such stews, I can hardly fail to hit on something tasty that agrees with me.”

“_Absit_,” said the doctor; “let no such base notion come near us! Nothing in the world provides poorer nourishment than an olla podrida. Save your ollas podridas for canons, or college rectors, or country weddings, but keep them off the tables of governors, where everything served should be delicate and refined. The reason is this: always, everywhere, and by everyone, simple medicines are valued above compound ones, because in the simple ones we cannot go wrong, while in the compound we can err merely by altering the proportions of their ingredients. What I believe the governor ought to eat now, to preserve and strengthen his health, is a hundred or so wafer cakes and a few thin slices of quince conserve, which will settle his stomach and aid his digestion.”
Hearing this, Sancho leaned back in his chair, looked the doctor over from head to foot, and in a grave voice asked him what his name was and where he had taken his studies.

He answered, “My name, señor governor, is Doctor Pedro Recio de Aguero. I come from a place called Tirteafuera, which lies between Caracuel and Almodóvar del Campo, on the right-hand side, and I hold my doctor's degree from the university of Osuna.”

At this Sancho, burning all over with fury, shot back, “Then let Doctor Pedro Recio de Malaguero, native of Tirteafuera — a place on the right-hand side as you travel from Caracuel to Almodóvar del Campo — graduate of Osuna, clear out of my sight this instant; or I swear by the sun I'll pick up a club and, starting with him, beat my way through every doctor on this island; at least every one I know to be ignorant, for learned, wise, sensible physicians I will honor and revere as if they were divine. I say it again: let Pedro Recio get out of here, or I'll take this chair I'm sitting on and smash it over his head. And if I'm called to answer for it, I'll acquit myself by saying I did God a service in killing a bad doctor — a public executioner. Now bring me something to eat, or else take back your government; a trade that won't feed the man who works it isn't worth two beans.”

The doctor was alarmed to see the governor in such a rage, and he would have made his own Tirteafuera straight out of the room had not a post-horn sounded in the street at that very moment; the carver, leaning his head out the window, turned back and announced, “It's a courier from my lord the duke — no doubt carrying some dispatch of importance.”

The courier entered, sweating and out of breath, and drawing a paper from inside his shirt, placed it in the governor's hands. Sancho passed it to the majordomo and told him to read the address, which ran as follows:
_To Don Sancho Panza, Governor of the Island of Barataria, to be delivered into his own hands or those of his secretary._

Hearing this, Sancho asked, “Which of you is my secretary?” “I am, señor,” said one of those in attendance, “for I can read and write, and I am a Biscayan.” “With that qualification thrown in,” said Sancho, “you could be secretary to the emperor himself; open this paper and see what it says.” The newly minted secretary did so, and after reading the contents declared it a matter to be dealt with in private. Sancho ordered the room cleared, keeping back only the majordomo and the carver; the doctor and the rest withdrew, and the secretary then read out the letter, which said:

It has reached my ears, Señor Don Sancho Panza, that certain enemies of mine and of the island intend to launch a furious assault on it some night — which night, I cannot say. You must stay alert and keep watch, so they do not catch you off guard. I also know through reliable spies that four men have slipped into the town in disguise to take your life, because they fear your great abilities; keep your eyes open, be wary of anyone who comes up to speak with you, and eat nothing that is set before you. I will see to it that help reaches you if you find yourself in trouble, but in everything you must act as your good judgment would lead one to expect. Written here, the sixteenth of August, at four in the morning.
Your friend, THE DUKE.

Sancho was astounded, and the bystanders pretended to be just as amazed; then, turning to the majordomo, he said, “The first thing we must do — and it must be done right now — is throw Doctor Recio into the lock-up; because if anybody means to kill me, it's him, and by the slowest and worst death there is, which is starvation.”

“And furthermore,” said the carver, “in my opinion your worship should eat nothing at all on this table, for the whole spread was a gift from some nuns; and as the saying goes, ‘behind the cross lurks the devil.’”

“I won't argue with that,” said Sancho; “so for now bring me a piece of bread and four pounds or so of grapes — no poison can hide in those; the plain truth is I cannot carry on without eating, and if we're to be ready for these battles hanging over us, we'd better be well provisioned, for it's the belly that keeps the heart going, not the heart the belly. And you, secretary, write back to my lord the duke and tell him that all his orders will be carried out to the letter, exactly as he commands; and convey to my lady the duchess that I kiss her hands, and beg her not to forget to send my letter and my bundle to my wife Teresa Panza by messenger — I'll count it a great kindness and will serve her in everything within my power; and while you're at it, you can slip in a kiss of the hand for my master Don Quixote, so he may see that I'm grateful bread; and being a good secretary and a good Biscayan, you may add whatever you please and whatever fits best. Now clear away this cloth and give me something to eat, and I'll be ready for every spy and assassin and enchanter that comes against me or my island.”
At that moment a page entered and announced, “There is a farmer here on business who wishes to speak with your lordship about a matter of great importance, so he says.”

“It's a strange thing,” said Sancho, “these men and their business; can they really be such fools as not to see that an hour like this is no hour for business calls? We who govern, we who sit as judges — aren't we men of flesh and blood? Aren't we entitled to the rest our bodies need, or would they have us carved out of marble? By God and on my conscience, if this government stays in my hands (and I have a feeling it won't), I'll bring more than one of these business callers to heel. Still, tell the good man to come in; but first make sure he isn't one of those spies, or one of my assassins.”
“No, my lord,” said the page, “he doesn't seem that sort, for he looks a simple soul, and either I know nothing at all or he's as good as good bread.”
“There is nothing to fear,” said the majordomo, “for all of us are here with you.”
“Carver,” said Sancho, “now that Doctor Pedro Recio is out of the room, would it be possible for me to eat something solid and substantial — even if it were only a piece of bread and an onion?”
“Tonight at supper,” said the carver, “everything the dinner lacked shall be made up, and your lordship will be left fully satisfied.”
“God willing,” said Sancho.
The farmer now came in — a fine-looking man whom you could tell from a thousand leagues away was an honest fellow and a good soul. The first thing he asked was, “Which one here is the lord governor?”
“Who else would it be,” said the secretary, “but the man seated in the chair?”

“Then I humble myself before him,” said the farmer; and dropping to his knees, he begged for the governor's hand to kiss. Sancho refused it and told him to get up and state his business. The farmer obeyed, and then said, “I am a farmer, señor, born in Miguelturra, a village two leagues from Ciudad Real.”
“Another Tirteafuera!” said Sancho; “go on, brother; I know Miguelturra well enough, I can tell you, for it isn't far from my own town.”

“The matter is this, señor,” the farmer continued: “by God's mercy I am married, with the leave and license of the holy Roman Catholic Church; I have two sons, both students — the younger studying for his bachelor's degree, the elder for his licentiate. I am a widower, for my wife died, or to put it more accurately, a bad doctor killed her on my hands by giving her a purge while she was with child; and if it had pleased God for the child to be born, and a boy, I would have set him to study to be a doctor, so he wouldn't have to envy his brothers the bachelor and the licentiate.”
“So if your wife hadn't died — or hadn't been killed — you wouldn't be a widower now,” said Sancho.
“No, señor, of course not,” said the farmer.
“Well, that much we've established,” said Sancho; “press on, brother, for this is an hour better suited to bed than to business.”

“Well then,” the farmer went on, “this son of mine who is to be the bachelor fell in love, in that same town, with a young lady named Clara Perlerina, daughter of Andres Perlerino, a very wealthy farmer; and this name Perlerines doesn't come to them through lineage or descent, but because the whole family suffers from palsy, and to dress it up they're called the Perlerines; though truth to tell, the young lady is fair as an Oriental pearl, like a flower of the field — when seen from the right side, that is; from the left, not so much, since on that side she's missing an eye she lost to smallpox; and although her face is thickly and deeply pockmarked, those who love her insist they're not pockmarks at all, but graves where the hearts of her suitors lie buried. She is so clean that, to keep from dirtying her face, she carries her nose tipped up, as the saying goes, so you'd swear it was running away from her mouth; and even so she looks remarkably well, because she has a wide mouth; and if she weren't short ten or a dozen teeth and grinders, she could stand comparison and competition with the loveliest of them. Of her lips I'll say nothing, for they're so fine and thin that if lips could be wound like thread, you could make a skein of them; but being a different color from ordinary lips, they're a marvel to behold — mottled blue, green, and purple. Let my lord the governor forgive me for painting in such detail the charms of one who sooner or later will be my daughter; for I love her, and to my eye there's nothing wrong with her.”
“Paint away as you please,” said Sancho; “the painting suits me, and if I had dined, no dessert could please my palate better than your portrait.”

“The portrait is one thing I still owe you,” said the farmer; “but the time will come when we'll manage what we can't manage now; and let me tell you, señor, if I could capture her grace and the height of her figure, it would amaze you; but that can't be done, because she's bent double, with her knees drawn up to her mouth; even so, anyone can see that if she could only stand upright, her head would knock against the ceiling; and she would already have given her hand in marriage to my bachelor, except that she can't stretch it out, being contracted as it is; yet even so, its long furrowed nails show how elegant and finely formed it is.”
“That will do, brother,” said Sancho; “consider her painted from head to foot. Now what is it you want? Come to the point without all this winding about, all these scraps and trimmings.”

“What I want, señor,” said the farmer, “is for your worship to do me the favor of a letter of recommendation to the girl's father, asking him to be so kind as to allow this marriage to go forward, since we are not badly matched, either in the gifts of fortune or in those of nature; for to tell you the truth, señor governor, my son is possessed by a devil, and not a day passes but the evil spirits torment him three or four times; and from having once fallen into the fire, his face is puckered up like a scrap of parchment, and his eyes are watery and forever running; but he has the temperament of an angel, and if he didn't thrash and pummel himself, he'd be a saint.”
“Is there anything more you want, good man?” asked Sancho.

“There is one more thing I'd ask,” said the farmer, “though I hardly dare mention it; but out it must come; after all, I can't let it sit rotting in my breast, whatever happens. What I mean, señor, is that I'd like your worship to give me three hundred or six hundred ducats toward my bachelor's marriage portion — to help him set up house; because they really must live on their own, free of the meddling of their fathers-in-law.”
“Think hard whether there's anything else you'd like,” said Sancho, “and don't be shy or modest about naming it.”
“No, truly, there is nothing,” said the farmer.

The instant he said it, the governor leaped to his feet, snatched up the chair he had been sitting in, and bellowed, “By all that's holy, you ill-mannered, clodhopping Don Bumpkin, if you don't clear out of here this second and get out of my sight, I'll split your head open with this chair. You whoreson scoundrel, you painter for the devil himself — at this hour you come asking me for six hundred ducats! Where would I get them, you stinking brute? And why would I give them to you if I had them, you knave, you blockhead? What do I care about Miguelturra or the whole tribe of the Perlerines? Out, I say, or by the life of my lord the duke I'll make good on my word. You're no man of Miguelturra — you're some rogue sent up from hell to tempt me. Why, you villain, I haven't held this government half a day, and already you want six hundred ducats out of me!”

The carver signaled the farmer to leave the room, which he did with his head hanging, looking for all the world terrified that the governor would make good on his threats — for the rogue knew very well how to play his part.

But let us leave Sancho to his fury, and peace be with the whole company; and let us return to Don Quixote, whom we left with his face bandaged and dressed after the cat wounds, which took eight full days to heal; and on one of those days there befell him something that Cide Hamete promises to recount with all the exactness and truthfulness he brings to every detail of this great history, however small it may be.
